It is Meccan entirely, according to al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAta' and Jabir.

It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah that it is Meccan except for one verse, which is His saying: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us.﴾ It is the first of the mufassal (the short surahs at the end of the Qur'an) according to the sound view, and it has been said that it begins from the surah of al-Hujurat.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "Surat Qaf was revealed in Makkah." Ibn Mardawayh narrated the like of it from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Muslim and others narrated from Qutbah ibn Malik who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite in the first rak'ah of the Fajr prayer ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾."

Ahmad, Muslim and the authors of the Sunan narrated from Abu Waqid al-Laythi who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite in the ʿId prayers ﴿Qaf﴾ and ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Umm Hisham bint Harithah who said: "I did not learn ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾ except from the mouth of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); he used to recite it every Friday on the pulpit when he addressed the people." It is in Sahih Muslim.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.

His saying: ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾. The discussion of the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of this is like the discussion we have already given regarding His saying: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an full of reminder﴾ [Sad: 1], and regarding His saying: ﴿Ha Mim. By the Book that makes things clear﴾ [az-Zukhruf and ad-Dukhan: 1, 2].

Regarding the meaning of (Qaf) there is difference of opinion. Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said it is the name of a mountain that encompasses the world, made of emerald, and the sky is domed over it, and it is beyond the veil behind which the sun sets, at a distance of a year's journey.

Al-Farra' said: "On this view the i'rab should appear on (Qaf), since it is a noun and not a spelled letter-name." He said: "Perhaps only the letter qaf was mentioned from its name, like the saying of the speaker: 'I said to her: stop (qifi), and she said: qaf', meaning: I am stopping."

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj related that some people said the meaning of (Qaf) is: "The matter has been decreed, and what is to occur has been decreed," just as it was said regarding (Ha Mim): "The matter has been decided (hummal-amr)."

It has been said that it is one of the names of Allah, by which He swore.

Qatadah said it is one of the names of the Qur'an.

al-Sha'bi said it is the opening of the surah.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said its meaning is: "Stop at Our command and Our prohibition and do not transgress them." It has also been said other things that are weaker than this.

The truth is that it is among the mutashabih (ambiguous matters) whose knowledge Allah has reserved for Himself, as we verified in the opening of Surat al-Baqarah. The meaning of (al-Majid) is that it possesses glory and nobility above all the revealed books.

Al-Hasan said: "the Generous." It has been said: "the one of high rank," and it has been said: "the one of great rank."

As for the response to the oath: the Kufans said it is His saying: ﴿Nay, they wonder﴾. Al-Akhfash said its response is omitted, as if he said: "Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an, you will surely be resurrected," indicated by ﴿When we die and become dust?﴾. Ibn Kaysan said its response is ﴿What word he utters is not but with a watchful observer beside him﴾ [Qaf: 18]. It has also been said it is ﴿We certainly know what the earth diminishes of them﴾ with the lam implied: that is, "indeed We know." It has also been said that it is omitted, and its estimate is: "We sent it down to you so that you may warn," as if it were said: "Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an, We sent it down to you so that you may warn the people by it."

The majority recited qāf with sukūn.

al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Nasr ibn ʿAsim read it with kasrah on the fa'.

ʿIsa al-Thaqafi read it with fatḥah on the fa'; Harun and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read it with ḍammah.

2 - ﴿Nay, they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them.﴾ Bal (nay) here is a turning away from the response, according to the differing opinions, and (an) is in a position of naṣb (accusative), with the estimate: "because a warner has come to them."

The meaning: Nay, the disbelievers wondered that a warner from among themselves came to them, and that warner is Muhammad (ﷺ). They did not content themselves with mere doubt and rejection; rather they made it one of the strange matters. It has also been said that it is a turning away from describing the Qur'an as glorious, and the explanation of this has already passed in Surat Sad.

Then He explained what He related of them, that they wondered, by His saying: ﴿So the disbelievers said: This is a strange thing.﴾ In it there is an additional explicitness and clarification.

Qatadah said: their wonder was that they were called to one God. It has also been said their wonder was at the resurrection.

So the word (this) refers to something unspecified which is explained by what follows it, His saying: ﴿When we die...﴾ etc. The first is more preferable.

al-Razi said: "The apparent meaning is that their saying 'this' refers to the coming of the warner, then they said: ﴿When we die...﴾. Also, here after the astonishment expressed by the interrogative, there occurred a matter that conveys the meaning of wonder, namely their saying: ﴿That is a far-off return﴾, for it is astonishment and is like wonder. So if the wonder expressed by their saying: ﴿This is a strange thing﴾ returned to their saying 'when' (idha), it would be like repetition. If it is said: explicit repetition necessarily follows from your saying 'this is a strange thing' that it refers to the coming of the warner, since their wonder at it was known from their saying 'and they wondered that he came to them'; so His saying 'this is a strange thing' would be a repetition. We say: that is not repetition but confirmation, because when He said 'Nay, they wonder' in the verbal form, and it is possible for a person to wonder at what is not a wonder, as in His saying: ﴿Do you wonder at the command of Allah?﴾ [Hud: 73], and it is said in common usage: 'There is no reason for your wondering at what is not wonderful', so when they wondered it was said to them: there is no sense in your wondering; so they said: ﴿This is a strange thing﴾ — how then should we not wonder at it? This is shown by His saying here ﴿So the disbelievers said﴾ with the fa', for it indicates that it is consequent upon what preceded."

The majority recited ﴿When we die...﴾ with the interrogative.

Ibn ʿAmir in one narration from him, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Aʿmash and al-Aʿraj read it with a single hamzah, so it may be interrogative as in the reading of the majority, with the interrogative hamzah implied, and it may be that its meaning is declarative.

The governing element of the adverb (idha) is implied: that is, "will He resurrect us?" or "will we return when we die?", indicated by what follows it, according to the reading of the majority. As for the second reading, the response of (idha) is omitted, that is: "we have returned"; it has been said: "that is a return." The meaning: their denial of resurrection after their death and their becoming dust.

Then they firmly judged their denial of resurrection, saying: "That, i.e., the resurrection, is ﴿a far-off return﴾," that is, far from the intellects, or the understandings, or the custom, or possibility. It is said: "I returned him, I return him, a returning," and "he returned, he returns, a return."

Then He, glorified be He, refuted what they said, saying: ﴿We certainly know what the earth diminishes of them﴾, that is, what it eats of their bodies, so nothing of that is lost to Us. And one whose knowledge encompasses everything, to the extent that it reaches the knowledge of what departs from the bodies of the dead in the graves, will not find resurrection difficult nor consider it far-fetched. al-Suddi said: "the diminishing here is death; He says: We know who dies among them and who remains, for whoever dies is buried, so it is as if the earth diminishes from the dead." It has also been said the meaning is: whoever among the polytheists enters Islam. The first is preferable. ﴿And with Us is a Book preserved﴾, that is, one that preserves their number and their names and everything among things; it is the Preserved Tablet, that is, guarded from the devils, or in which everything is preserved.

Then He, glorified be He, turned away from their first speech and moved to what is more heinous than it, saying: ﴿Nay, they denied the truth﴾, for it is an explicit statement from them of denial after what had preceded from them of mockery. The truth here means the Qur'an. al-Mawardi said: "according to all," and it has been said it is Islam, and it has been said it is Muhammad, and it has been said it is prophethood established by miracles. ﴿When it came to them﴾, that is, at the time of its coming to them, without reflection, without contemplation, and without close examination.

The majority read ﴿lamma﴾ with fatḥah on the lam and tashdid on the mim. al-Jahdari read it with kasrah on the lam and takhfif on the mim.

﴿So they are in a confused matter﴾, that is, mixed up and disturbed: they say at one time "sorcerer," at another "poet," and at another "soothsayer." Said by al-Zajjaj and others.

Qatadah said: "differing."

al-Hasan said: "confused." The meanings are close. It has been said: "corrupt," and the meanings are close.

From it is their saying: "the trusts of people became marij," i.e., corrupted, and "the religion and the matter marija," i.e., became mixed.

﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, that is: how did they neglect looking at the sky above them ﴿how We built it﴾ and made it in this description, raised without a pillar upon which it rests ﴿and adorned it﴾ with what We placed in it of lamps ﴿and it has no rifts﴾, that is, openings, cracks, and fissures. It is the plural of farj, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays: "He closes with it her gap from behind." al-Kisa'i said: "there is no disparity in it, no difference, and no openings."

﴿And the earth — We spread it out﴾, that is, We extended it, ﴿and cast into it firm mountains﴾, that is, stable mountains; the explanation of this has already passed in Surat al-Ra'd. ﴿And We caused to grow in it of every beautiful pair﴾, that is, of every good kind; the explanation of this has already passed in Surat al-Hajj.

﴿As an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back in repentance.﴾ These two are causes for what preceded, governed by the last verb of them, or by an implied one: that is, "We did what We did for insight and remembrance," as said by al-Zajjaj. Abu Hatim said: "they are in the accusative as verbal nouns (masdar), that is: We made that an insight and a reminder."

Al-Munib is the one who returns to Allah in repentance, who reflects upon the wonder of His creation and the marvels of His creatures.

In the context of this verse there is a reminder to those who deny resurrection, and an awakening for them from the course of heedlessness, and an explanation of the possibility of that and of its not being impossible, for whoever is capable of such matters is capable of it.

Likewise His saying: ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water﴾, that is, We sent down from the clouds water of abundant blessing, for people's benefit in most of their affairs. ﴿And We caused to grow by it gardens﴾, that is, We caused by that water many gardens to grow, ﴿and grain of the harvest﴾, that is, what is eaten as food and harvested of grains; the meaning is: the grain of the harvested crop, and the grain was singled out because it is the intended object. So said the Basrans. The Kufans said: it is from the genre of the attribution of a thing to itself, like "the congregational mosque," related by al-Farra'. al-Dahhak said: "the grain of the harvest is wheat and barley." It has been said: every grain that is harvested, stored, and eaten.

﴿And the tall palm trees, having fruit-clusters stacked one upon another﴾. It is coordinated with (gardens): that is, and We caused to grow by it the palm trees. Its singling out by mention, despite its inclusion among the gardens, is to indicate its excellence over the rest of the trees. The accusative of (bāsiqāt) is as a circumstantial state, and it is a presumed state, since at the time of growing they were not yet tall.

Mujahid, ʿIkrimah and Qatadah said: the bāsiqāt are the tall ones. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: "upright."

al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah and al-Farra' said: "heavy with fruit, pregnant," it is said of a she-goat when she bāsaqat: she gave birth. The more well-known in the language of the Arabs is the first. It is said: "the palm tree basaqat busuqan," when it grew tall. From it is the saying of the poet:

"For us is wine, but not the wine of a vineyard,
but from the produce of the tall palms,
noble in the sky, they have gone tall,
and their fruits have escaped the hands of the pickers."

The clause ﴿having fruit-clusters stacked one upon another﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial state of the palm trees. The ṭalʿ is the first thing that emerges from the fruit of the palm; it is said: "the ṭalʿ emerged, ṭuluʿan." The naḍīd is what is layered, one part stacked upon another, and that is before it opens; so it is naḍīd within its sheaths, and when it emerges from its sheaths it is no longer naḍīd.

﴿A provision for the servants﴾: its accusative is as a verbal noun, that is, "We provided them a provision," or as a reason, that is, "We caused these things to grow for provision." ﴿And We revived by it a dead land﴾, that is, We revived by that water a barren land having no fruit or crop. The clause ﴿Thus will be the emergence﴾ is a new sentence explaining that the emergence from the graves at the resurrection is like this revival by which Allah revived the dead earth. The majority read mayta with light pronunciation; Abu Jaʿfar and Khalid read it with heavy pronunciation.

Then He, glorified be He, mentioned the nations that denied, saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, and the companions of the Rass﴾. They are the people of Shuʿayb, as its explanation has already passed. It has been said they are those to whom there came from the farthest part of the city a man running; and they are from the people of ʿIsa. It has also been said they are the People of the Trench.

Al-Rass is either a place they were named after, or a verb, which is digging a well; it is said "rassa" when he dug a well.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 50, verses 1–15 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And Thamud﴾, ﴿and 'Ad, and Pharaoh﴾, meaning Pharaoh and his people, ﴿and the brothers of Lut﴾. He called them his brothers because they were his in-laws. It was also said that they were from the people of Ibrahim, and that they were acquaintances of Lut.

﴿And the companions of the Thicket﴾. The discussion of the Thicket (al-Aykah) and the differences of the readers (qurra') concerning it has already been covered in full in Surat ash-Shu'ara'. Their prophet, whom Allah sent to them, was Shu'ayb. ﴿And the people of Tubba'﴾. Tubba' is al-Himyari, the one previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'?﴾ [al-Dukhan: 37]. His name was Sa'd Abu Karib, and it was said that it was As'ad. Qatadah said: "Allah censured the people of Tubba', and He did not censure him."

﴿Each one denied the Messengers﴾. The tanwin (nunation) here is a substitute for the omitted genitive noun that follows: that is, each one of these peoples denied its own messenger whom Allah had sent to it, and denied what he had brought of the Law. The lam in (al-Rusul), "the Messengers," may be the lam of specific reference (al-'ahd), or it may be the lam of genus (al-jins): that is, each of these groups denied all the Messengers. The singular pronoun in (kadhdhaba), "he denied," is in keeping with the singular form of the word (kull), "each." In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as if it were said to him: Do not grieve, and do not let your sorrow increase over the denial of these people toward you. This is the condition of those prophets who came before you, for their peoples denied them, and only a few of them believed. ﴿So the threat of Mine came into effect﴾, meaning My threat became binding upon them, the word of punishment was fulfilled against them, and there befell them what Allah had decreed for them of sinking into the earth, transformation, and destruction by the various kinds of punishment that Allah sent down upon them.

﴿Were We then weary with the first creation?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, and the sentence is a new clause establishing the matter of resurrection, which the peoples denied. That is: Were We incapable with creation when We created them first, when they were nothing? Then how would We be incapable of resurrecting them? It is said: "'ayiytu bi-l-amr" means "I was unable to do the matter and did not know its way."

The majority of readers (qara') read (ʾafa-ʿayiyna), with a kasrah on the first yaʾ followed by a silent yaʾ.
Ibn Abi 'Abla read it with a shaddah on the yaʾ, without ishbaʿ (elongation).

Then He mentioned that they are in doubt about resurrection, and said: ﴿Nay, but they are in confusion regarding a new creation﴾, meaning they are in doubt, bewilderment, and confusion concerning a fresh creation, which is the raising of the dead. The meaning of the idrab (the turn to a new point, "nay") is that they do not deny Allah's power over the first creation. ﴿Nay, but they are in confusion regarding a new creation﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Qaf﴾, that he said: "It is one of the names of Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: Allah created, beyond this earth, a surrounding sea. Then He created beyond that a mountain called "Qaf," with the lowest heaven fluttering over it. Then He created beyond that mountain an earth like this earth, seven times over. Then He created beyond that a surrounding sea encompassing them. Then He created beyond that a mountain called "Qaf," with the second heaven fluttering over it. And so he counted seven earths, seven seas, seven mountains, and seven heavens. He said: This is His saying: ﴿And the sea, with seven seas behind it to replenish it﴾ [Luqman: 27]. Ibn Kathir said: Its chain of transmission is not sound from Ibn 'Abbas. He also said: There is a break in it.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, also, that he said: It is a mountain, and its veins extend to the rock upon which the earth rests. So when Allah wills to shake a town, He commands that mountain, and it moves that vein which is adjacent to that town, and it shakes and quakes it. This is why He shakes one town and not another.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also, regarding ﴿And the glorious Qur'an﴾, that he said: "Glorious" means "noble."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also, that he said: The glorious Qur'an — there is nothing better or more excellent than it.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also, regarding ﴿We know what the earth diminishes of them﴾, that he said: Their bodies, and what goes away from them.

Ibn Jarir narrated from him, also, concerning the verse, that he said: What it eats of their flesh, their bones, and their hair.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, also, that he said: "Marij" is a thing that has changed.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Qutbah, who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) reciting in the dawn prayer (Surah) Qaf. When he reached this verse, ﴿And the tall palm trees﴾, I began to say: What is its basuq? He said: Its height."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And the tall palm trees﴾, that he said: "Height."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿For it are clusters of spathes, layered﴾, that he said: "Piled one upon another."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also, regarding His saying ﴿Were We then weary with the first creation?﴾, that he said: "The first creation did not weary Us." The governing element of the adverb (idha) is implied: that is, "will He resurrect us?" or "will we return when we die?", indicated by what follows it, according to the reading of the majority. As for the second reading, the response of (idha) is omitted, that is: "we have returned"; it has been said: "that is a return." The meaning: their denial of resurrection after their death and their becoming dust.

Then they firmly judged their denial of resurrection, saying: "That, i.e., the resurrection, is ﴿a far-off return﴾," that is, far from the intellects, or the understandings, or the custom, or possibility. It is said: "I returned him, I return him, a returning," and "he returned, he returns, a return."

Then He, glorified be He, refuted what they said, saying: ﴿We certainly know what the earth diminishes of them﴾, that is, what it eats of their bodies, so nothing of that is lost to Us. And one whose knowledge encompasses everything, to the extent that it reaches the knowledge of what departs from the bodies of the dead in the graves, will not find resurrection difficult nor consider it far-fetched. al-Suddi said: "the diminishing here is death; He says: We know who dies among them and who remains, for whoever dies is buried, so it is as if the earth diminishes from the dead." It has also been said the meaning is: whoever among the polytheists enters Islam. The first is preferable. ﴿And with Us is a Book preserved﴾, that is, one that preserves their number and their names and everything among things; it is the Preserved Tablet, that is, guarded from the devils, or in which everything is preserved.

Then He, glorified be He, turned away from their first speech and moved to what is more heinous than it, saying: ﴿Nay, they denied the truth﴾, for it is an explicit statement from them of denial after what had preceded from them of mockery. The truth here means the Qur'an. al-Mawardi said: "according to all," and it has been said it is Islam, and it has been said it is Muhammad, and it has been said it is prophethood established by miracles. ﴿When it came to them﴾, that is, at the time of its coming to them, without reflection, without contemplation, and without close examination.

The majority read ﴿lamma﴾ with fatḥah on the lam and tashdid on the mim. al-Jahdari read it with kasrah on the lam and takhfif on the mim.

﴿So they are in a confused matter﴾, that is, mixed up and disturbed: they say at one time "sorcerer," at another "poet," and at another "soothsayer." Said by al-Zajjaj and others.

Qatadah said: "differing."

al-Hasan said: "confused." The meanings are close. It has been said: "corrupt," and the meanings are close.

From it is their saying: "the trusts of people became marij," i.e., corrupted, and "the religion and the matter marija," i.e., became mixed.

﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, that is: how did they neglect looking at the sky above them ﴿how We built it﴾ and made it in this description, raised without a pillar upon which it rests ﴿and adorned it﴾ with what We placed in it of lamps ﴿and it has no rifts﴾, that is, openings, cracks, and fissures. It is the plural of farj, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays: "He closes with it her gap from behind." al-Kisa'i said: "there is no disparity in it, no difference, and no openings."

﴿And the earth — We spread it out﴾, that is, We extended it, ﴿and cast into it firm mountains﴾, that is, stable mountains; the explanation of this has already passed in Surat al-Ra'd. ﴿And We caused to grow in it of every beautiful pair﴾, that is, of every good kind; the explanation of this has already passed in Surat al-Hajj.

﴿As an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back in repentance.﴾ These two are causes for what preceded, governed by the last verb of them, or by an implied one: that is, "We did what We did for insight and remembrance," as said by al-Zajjaj. Abu Hatim said: "they are in the accusative as verbal nouns (masdar), that is: We made that an insight and a reminder."

Al-Munib is the one who returns to Allah in repentance, who reflects upon the wonder of His creation and the marvels of His creatures.

In the context of this verse there is a reminder to those who deny resurrection, and an awakening for them from the course of heedlessness, and an explanation of the possibility of that and of its not being impossible, for whoever is capable of such matters is capable of it.

Likewise His saying: ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water﴾, that is, We sent down from the clouds water of abundant blessing, for people's benefit in most of their affairs. ﴿And We caused to grow by it gardens﴾, that is, We caused by that water many gardens to grow, ﴿and grain of the harvest﴾, that is, what is eaten as food and harvested of grains; the meaning is: the grain of the harvested crop, and the grain was singled out because it is the intended object. So said the Basrans. The Kufans said: it is from the genre of the attribution of a thing to itself, like "the congregational mosque," related by al-Farra'. al-Dahhak said: "the grain of the harvest is wheat and barley." It has been said: every grain that is harvested, stored, and eaten.

﴿And the tall palm trees, having fruit-clusters stacked one upon another﴾. It is coordinated with (gardens): that is, and We caused to grow by it the palm trees. Its singling out by mention, despite its inclusion among the gardens, is to indicate its excellence over the rest of the trees. The accusative of (bāsiqāt) is as a circumstantial state, and it is a presumed state, since at the time of growing they were not yet tall.

Mujahid, ʿIkrimah and Qatadah said: the bāsiqāt are the tall ones. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: "upright."

al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah and al-Farra' said: "heavy with fruit, pregnant," it is said of a she-goat when she bāsaqat: she gave birth. The more well-known in the language of the Arabs is the first. It is said: "the palm tree basaqat busuqan," when it grew tall. From it is the saying of the poet:

"For us is wine, but not the wine of a vineyard,
but from the produce of the tall palms,
noble in the sky, they have gone tall,
and their fruits have escaped the hands of the pickers."

The clause ﴿having fruit-clusters stacked one upon another﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial state of the palm trees. The ṭalʿ is the first thing that emerges from the fruit of the palm; it is said: "the ṭalʿ emerged, ṭuluʿan." The naḍīd is what is layered, one part stacked upon another, and that is before it opens; so it is naḍīd within its sheaths, and when it emerges from its sheaths it is no longer naḍīd.

﴿A provision for the servants﴾: its accusative is as a verbal noun, that is, "We provided them a provision," or as a reason, that is, "We caused these things to grow for provision." ﴿And We revived by it a dead land﴾, that is, We revived by that water a barren land having no fruit or crop. The clause ﴿Thus will be the emergence﴾ is a new sentence explaining that the emergence from the graves at the resurrection is like this revival by which Allah revived the dead earth. The majority read mayta with light pronunciation; Abu Jaʿfar and Khalid read it with heavy pronunciation.

Then He, glorified be He, mentioned the nations that denied, saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, and the companions of the Rass﴾. They are the people of Shuʿayb, as its explanation has already passed. It has been said they are those to whom there came from the farthest part of the city a man running; and they are from the people of ʿIsa. It has also been said they are the People of the Trench.

Al-Rass is either a place they were named after, or a verb, which is digging a well; it is said "rassa" when he dug a well.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 50, verses 1–15 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And Thamud﴾, ﴿and 'Ad, and Pharaoh﴾, meaning Pharaoh and his people, ﴿and the brothers of Lut﴾. He called them his brothers because they were his in-laws. It was also said that they were from the people of Ibrahim, and that they were acquaintances of Lut.

﴿And the companions of the Thicket﴾. The discussion of the Thicket (al-Aykah) and the differences of the readers (qurra') concerning it has already been covered in full in Surat ash-Shu'ara'. Their prophet, whom Allah sent to them, was Shu'ayb. ﴿And the people of Tubba'﴾. Tubba' is al-Himyari, the one previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'?﴾ [al-Dukhan: 37]. His name was Sa'd Abu Karib, and it was said that it was As'ad. Qatadah said: "Allah censured the people of Tubba', and He did not censure him."

﴿Each one denied the Messengers﴾. The tanwin (nunation) here is a substitute for the omitted genitive noun that follows: that is, each one of these peoples denied its own messenger whom Allah had sent to it, and denied what he had brought of the Law. The lam in (al-Rusul), "the Messengers," may be the lam of specific reference (al-'ahd), or it may be the lam of genus (al-jins): that is, each of these groups denied all the Messengers. The singular pronoun in (kadhdhaba), "he denied," is in keeping with the singular form of the word (kull), "each." In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as if it were said to him: Do not grieve, and do not let your sorrow increase over the denial of these people toward you. This is the condition of those prophets who came before you, for their peoples denied them, and only a few of them believed. ﴿So the threat of Mine came into effect﴾, meaning My threat became binding upon them, the word of punishment was fulfilled against them, and there befell them what Allah had decreed for them of sinking into the earth, transformation, and destruction by the various kinds of punishment that Allah sent down upon them.

﴿Were We then weary with the first creation?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, and the sentence is a new clause establishing the matter of resurrection, which the peoples denied. That is: Were We incapable with creation when We created them first, when they were nothing? Then how would We be incapable of resurrecting them? It is said: "'ayiytu bi-l-amr" means "I was unable to do the matter and did not know its way."

The majority of readers (qara') read (ʾafa-ʿayiyna), with a kasrah on the first yaʾ followed by a silent yaʾ.
Ibn Abi 'Abla read it with a shaddah on the yaʾ, without ishbaʿ (elongation).

Then He mentioned that they are in doubt about resurrection, and said: ﴿Nay, but they are in confusion regarding a new creation﴾, meaning they are in doubt, bewilderment, and confusion concerning a fresh creation, which is the raising of the dead. The meaning of the idrab (the turn to a new point, "nay") is that they do not deny Allah's power over the first creation. ﴿Nay, but they are in confusion regarding a new creation﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Qaf﴾, that he said: "It is one of the names of Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: Allah created, beyond this earth, a surrounding sea. Then He created beyond that a mountain called "Qaf," with the lowest heaven fluttering over it. Then He created beyond that mountain an earth like this earth, seven times over. Then He created beyond that a surrounding sea encompassing them. Then He created beyond that a mountain called "Qaf," with the second heaven fluttering over it. And so he counted seven earths, seven seas, seven mountains, and seven heavens. He said: This is His saying: ﴿And the sea, with seven seas behind it to replenish it﴾ [Luqman: 27]. Ibn Kathir said: Its chain of transmission is not sound from Ibn 'Abbas. He also said: There is a break in it.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, also, that he said: It is a mountain, and its veins extend to the rock upon which the earth rests. So when Allah wills to shake a town, He commands that mountain, and it moves that vein which is adjacent to that town, and it shakes and quakes it. This is why He shakes one town and not another.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also, regarding ﴿And the glorious Qur'an﴾, that he said: "Glorious" means "noble."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also, that he said: The glorious Qur'an — there is nothing better or more excellent than it.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also, regarding ﴿We know what the earth diminishes of them﴾, that he said: Their bodies, and what goes away from them.

Ibn Jarir narrated from him, also, concerning the verse, that he said: What it eats of their flesh, their bones, and their hair.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, also, that he said: "Marij" is a thing that has changed.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Qutbah, who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) reciting in the dawn prayer (Surah) Qaf. When he reached this verse, ﴿And the tall palm trees﴾, I began to say: What is its basuq? He said: Its height."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And the tall palm trees﴾, that he said: "Height."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿For it are clusters of spathes, layered﴾, that he said: "Piled one upon another."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also, regarding His saying ﴿Were We then weary with the first creation?﴾, that he said: "The first creation did not weary Us." And regarding His saying ﴿Nay, but they are in confusion regarding a new creation﴾, that he said: "They are in doubt about resurrection."

It is Meccan entirely, according to al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAta' and Jabir.

It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah that it is Meccan except for one verse, which is His saying: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us.﴾ It is the first of the mufassal (the short surahs at the end of the Qur'an) according to the sound view, and it has been said that it begins from the surah of al-Hujurat.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "Surat Qaf was revealed in Makkah." Ibn Mardawayh narrated the like of it from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Muslim and others narrated from Qutbah ibn Malik who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite in the first rak'ah of the Fajr prayer ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾."

Ahmad, Muslim and the authors of the Sunan narrated from Abu Waqid al-Laythi who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite in the ʿId prayers ﴿Qaf﴾ and ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Umm Hisham bint Harithah who said: "I did not learn ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾ except from the mouth of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); he used to recite it every Friday on the pulpit when he addressed the people." It is in Sahih Muslim.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.

His saying: ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾. The discussion of the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of this is like the discussion we have already given regarding His saying: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an full of reminder﴾ [Sad: 1], and regarding His saying: ﴿Ha Mim. By the Book that makes things clear﴾ [az-Zukhruf and ad-Dukhan: 1, 2].

Regarding the meaning of (Qaf) there is difference of opinion. Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said it is the name of a mountain that encompasses the world, made of emerald, and the sky is domed over it, and it is beyond the veil behind which the sun sets, at a distance of a year's journey.

Al-Farra' said: "On this view the i'rab should appear on (Qaf), since it is a noun and not a spelled letter-name." He said: "Perhaps only the letter qaf was mentioned from its name, like the saying of the speaker: 'I said to her: stop (qifi), and she said: qaf', meaning: I am stopping."

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj related that some people said the meaning of (Qaf) is: "The matter has been decreed, and what is to occur has been decreed," just as it was said regarding (Ha Mim): "The matter has been decided (hummal-amr)."

It has been said that it is one of the names of Allah, by which He swore.

Qatadah said it is one of the names of the Qur'an.

al-Sha'bi said it is the opening of the surah.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said its meaning is: "Stop at Our command and Our prohibition and do not transgress them." It has also been said other things that are weaker than this.

The truth is that it is among the mutashabih (ambiguous matters) whose knowledge Allah has reserved for Himself, as we verified in the opening of Surat al-Baqarah. The meaning of (al-Majid) is that it possesses glory and nobility above all the revealed books.

Al-Hasan said: "the Generous." It has been said: "the one of high rank," and it has been said: "the one of great rank."

As for the response to the oath: the Kufans said it is His saying: ﴿Nay, they wonder﴾. Al-Akhfash said its response is omitted, as if he said: "Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an, you will surely be resurrected," indicated by ﴿When we die and become dust?﴾. Ibn Kaysan said its response is ﴿What word he utters is not but with a watchful observer beside him﴾ [Qaf: 18]. It has also been said it is ﴿We certainly know what the earth diminishes of them﴾ with the lam implied: that is, "indeed We know." It has also been said that it is omitted, and its estimate is: "We sent it down to you so that you may warn," as if it were said: "Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an, We sent it down to you so that you may warn the people by it."

The majority recited qāf with sukūn.

al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Nasr ibn ʿAsim read it with kasrah on the fa'.

ʿIsa al-Thaqafi read it with fatḥah on the fa'; Harun and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read it with ḍammah.

2 - ﴿Nay, they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them.﴾ Bal (nay) here is a turning away from the response, according to the differing opinions, and (an) is in a position of naṣb (accusative), with the estimate: "because a warner has come to them."

The meaning: Nay, the disbelievers wondered that a warner from among themselves came to them, and that warner is Muhammad (ﷺ). They did not content themselves with mere doubt and rejection; rather they made it one of the strange matters. It has also been said that it is a turning away from describing the Qur'an as glorious, and the explanation of this has already passed in Surat Sad.

Then He explained what He related of them, that they wondered, by His saying: ﴿So the disbelievers said: This is a strange thing.﴾ In it there is an additional explicitness and clarification.

Qatadah said: their wonder was that they were called to one God. It has also been said their wonder was at the resurrection.

So the word (this) refers to something unspecified which is explained by what follows it, His saying: ﴿When we die...﴾ etc. The first is more preferable.

al-Razi said: "The apparent meaning is that their saying 'this' refers to the coming of the warner, then they said: ﴿When we die...﴾. Also, here after the astonishment expressed by the interrogative, there occurred a matter that conveys the meaning of wonder, namely their saying: ﴿That is a far-off return﴾, for it is astonishment and is like wonder. Then He, glorified be He, mentioned the nations that denied, saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, and the companions of the Rass﴾. They are the people of Shuʿayb, as its explanation has already passed. It has been said they are those to whom there came from the farthest part of the city a man running; and they are from the people of ʿIsa. It has also been said they are the People of the Trench.

Al-Rass is either a place they were named after, or a verb, which is digging a well; it is said "rassa" when he dug a well.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 50, verses 1–15 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And Thamud﴾, ﴿and 'Ad, and Pharaoh﴾, meaning Pharaoh and his people, ﴿and the brothers of Lut﴾. He called them his brothers because they were his in-laws. It was also said that they were from the people of Ibrahim, and that they were acquaintances of Lut.

﴿And the companions of the Thicket﴾. The discussion of the Thicket (al-Aykah) and the differences of the readers (qurra') concerning it has already been covered in full in Surat ash-Shu'ara'. Their prophet, whom Allah sent to them, was Shu'ayb. ﴿And the people of Tubba'﴾. Tubba' is al-Himyari, the one previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'?﴾ [al-Dukhan: 37]. His name was Sa'd Abu Karib, and it was said that it was As'ad. Qatadah said: "Allah censured the people of Tubba', and He did not censure him."

﴿Each one denied the Messengers﴾. The tanwin (nunation) here is a substitute for the omitted genitive noun that follows: that is, each one of these peoples denied its own messenger whom Allah had sent to it, and denied what he had brought of the Law. The lam in (al-Rusul), "the Messengers," may be the lam of specific reference (al-'ahd), or it may be the lam of genus (al-jins): that is, each of these groups denied all the Messengers. The singular pronoun in (kadhdhaba), "he denied," is in keeping with the singular form of the word (kull), "each." In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as if it were said to him: Do not grieve, and do not let your sorrow increase over the denial of these people toward you. This is the condition of those prophets who came before you, for their peoples denied them, and only a few of them believed. ﴿So the threat of Mine came into effect﴾, meaning My threat became binding upon them, the word of punishment was fulfilled against them, and there befell them what Allah had decreed for them of sinking into the earth, transformation, and destruction by the various kinds of punishment that Allah sent down upon them.

﴿Were We then weary with the first creation?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, and the sentence is a new clause establishing the matter of resurrection, which the peoples denied. That is: Were We incapable with creation when We created them first, when they were nothing? Then how would We be incapable of resurrecting them? It is said: "'ayiytu bi-l-amr" means "I was unable to do the matter and did not know its way."

The majority of readers (qara') read (ʾafa-ʿayiyna), with a kasrah on the first yaʾ followed by a silent yaʾ.
Ibn Abi 'Abla read it with a shaddah on the yaʾ, without ishbaʿ (elongation).

Then He mentioned that they are in doubt about resurrection, and said: ﴿Nay, but they are in confusion regarding a new creation﴾, meaning they are in doubt, bewilderment, and confusion concerning a fresh creation, which is the raising of the dead. The meaning of the idrab (the turn to a new point, "nay") is that they do not deny Allah's power over the first creation. ﴿Nay, but they are in confusion regarding a new creation﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Qaf﴾, that he said: "It is one of the names of Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: Allah created, beyond this earth, a surrounding sea. Then He created beyond that a mountain called "Qaf," with the lowest heaven fluttering over it. Then He created beyond that mountain an earth like this earth, seven times over. Then He created beyond that a surrounding sea encompassing them. Then He created beyond that a mountain called "Qaf," with the second heaven fluttering over it. And so he counted seven earths, seven seas, seven mountains, and seven heavens. He said: This is His saying: ﴿And the sea, with seven seas behind it to replenish it﴾ [Luqman: 27]. Ibn Kathir said: Its chain of transmission is not sound from Ibn 'Abbas. He also said: There is a break in it.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, also, that he said: It is a mountain, and its veins extend to the rock upon which the earth rests. So when Allah wills to shake a town, He commands that mountain, and it moves that vein which is adjacent to that town, and it shakes and quakes it. This is why He shakes one town and not another.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also, regarding ﴿And the glorious Qur'an﴾, that he said: "Glorious" means "noble."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also, that he said: The glorious Qur'an — there is nothing better or more excellent than it.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also, regarding ﴿We know what the earth diminishes of them﴾, that he said: Their bodies, and what goes away from them.

Ibn Jarir narrated from him, also, concerning the verse, that he said: What it eats of their flesh, their bones, and their hair.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, also, that he said: "Marij" is a thing that has changed.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Qutbah, who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) reciting in the dawn prayer (Surah) Qaf. When he reached this verse, ﴿And the tall palm trees﴾, I began to say: What is its basuq? He said: Its height."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And the tall palm trees﴾, that he said: "Height."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿For it are clusters of spathes, layered﴾, that he said: "Piled one upon another."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also, regarding His saying ﴿Were We then weary with the first creation?﴾, that he said: "The first creation did not weary Us." And regarding His saying ﴿Nay, but they are in confusion regarding a new creation﴾, that he said: "They are in doubt about resurrection."

It is Meccan entirely, according to al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAta' and Jabir.

It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah that it is Meccan except for one verse, which is His saying: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us.﴾ It is the first of the mufassal (the short surahs at the end of the Qur'an) according to the sound view, and it has been said that it begins from the surah of al-Hujurat.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "Surat Qaf was revealed in Makkah." Ibn Mardawayh narrated the like of it from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Muslim and others narrated from Qutbah ibn Malik who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite in the first rak'ah of the Fajr prayer ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾."

Ahmad, Muslim and the authors of the Sunan narrated from Abu Waqid al-Laythi who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite in the ʿId prayers ﴿Qaf﴾ and ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Umm Hisham bint Harithah who said: "I did not learn ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾ except from the mouth of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); he used to recite it every Friday on the pulpit when he addressed the people." It is in Sahih Muslim.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.

His saying: ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾. The discussion of the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of this is like the discussion we have already given regarding His saying: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an full of reminder﴾ [Sad: 1], and regarding His saying: ﴿Ha Mim. By the Book that makes things clear﴾ [az-Zukhruf and ad-Dukhan: 1, 2].

Regarding the meaning of (Qaf) there is difference of opinion. Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said it is the name of a mountain that encompasses the world, made of emerald, and the sky is domed over it, and it is beyond the veil behind which the sun sets, at a distance of a year's journey.

Al-Farra' said: "On this view the i'rab should appear on (Qaf), since it is a noun and not a spelled letter-name." He said: "Perhaps only the letter qaf was mentioned from its name, like the saying of the speaker: 'I said to her: stop (qifi), and she said: qaf', meaning: I am stopping."

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj related that some people said the meaning of (Qaf) is: "The matter has been decreed, and what is to occur has been decreed," just as it was said regarding (Ha Mim): "The matter has been decided (hummal-amr)."

It has been said that it is one of the names of Allah, by which He swore.

Qatadah said it is one of the names of the Qur'an.

al-Sha'bi said it is the opening of the surah.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said its meaning is: "Stop at Our command and Our prohibition and do not transgress them." It has also been said other things that are weaker than this.

The truth is that it is among the mutashabih (ambiguous matters) whose knowledge Allah has reserved for Himself, as we verified in the opening of Surat al-Baqarah. The meaning of (al-Majid) is that it possesses glory and nobility above all the revealed books.

Al-Hasan said: "the Generous." It has been said: "the one of high rank," and it has been said: "the one of great rank."

As for the response to the oath: the Kufans said it is His saying: ﴿Nay, they wonder﴾. Al-Akhfash said its response is omitted, as if he said: "Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an, you will surely be resurrected," indicated by ﴿When we die and become dust?﴾. Ibn Kaysan said its response is ﴿What word he utters is not but with a watchful observer beside him﴾ [Qaf: 18]. It has also been said it is ﴿We certainly know what the earth diminishes of them﴾ with the lam implied: that is, "indeed We know." It has also been said that it is omitted, and its estimate is: "We sent it down to you so that you may warn," as if it were said: "Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an, We sent it down to you so that you may warn the people by it."

The majority recited qāf with sukūn.

al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Nasr ibn ʿAsim read it with kasrah on the fa'.

ʿIsa al-Thaqafi read it with fatḥah on the fa'; Harun and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read it with ḍammah.

2 - ﴿Nay, they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them.﴾ Bal (nay) here is a turning away from the response, according to the differing opinions, and (an) is in a position of naṣb (accusative), with the estimate: "because a warner has come to them."

The meaning: Nay, the disbelievers wondered that a warner from among themselves came to them, and that warner is Muhammad (ﷺ). They did not content themselves with mere doubt and rejection; rather they made it one of the strange matters. It has also been said that it is a turning away from describing the Qur'an as glorious, and the explanation of this has already passed in Surat Sad.

Then He explained what He related of them, that they wondered, by His saying: ﴿So the disbelievers said: This is a strange thing.﴾ In it there is an additional explicitness and clarification.

Qatadah said: their wonder was that they were called to one God. It has also been said their wonder was at the resurrection.

So the word (this) refers to something unspecified which is explained by what follows it, His saying: ﴿When we die...﴾ etc. The first is more preferable.

al-Razi said: "The apparent meaning is that their saying 'this' refers to the coming of the warner, then they said: ﴿When we die...﴾. Also, here after the astonishment expressed by the interrogative, there occurred a matter that conveys the meaning of wonder, namely their saying: ﴿That is a far-off return﴾, for it is astonishment and is like wonder. So if the wonder expressed by their saying: ﴿This is a strange thing﴾ returned to their saying 'when' (idha), it would be like repetition. If it is said: explicit repetition necessarily follows from your saying 'this is a strange thing' that it refers to the coming of the warner, since their wonder at it was known from their saying 'and they wondered that he came to them'; so His saying 'this is a strange thing' would be a repetition. We say: that is not repetition but confirmation, because when He said 'Nay, they wonder' in the verbal form, and it is possible for a person to wonder at what is not a wonder, as in His saying: ﴿Do you wonder at the command of Allah?﴾ [Hud: 73], and it is said in common usage: 'There is no reason for your wondering at what is not wonderful', so when they wondered it was said to them: there is no sense in your wondering; so they said: ﴿This is a strange thing﴾ — how then should we not wonder at it? This is shown by His saying here ﴿So the disbelievers said﴾ with the fa', for it indicates that it is consequent upon what preceded."

The majority recited ﴿When we die...﴾ with the interrogative.

Ibn ʿAmir in one narration from him, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Aʿmash and al-Aʿraj read it with a single hamzah, so it may be interrogative as in the reading of the majority, with the interrogative hamzah implied, and it may be that its meaning is declarative.

The governing element of the adverb (idha) is implied: that is, "will He resurrect us?" or "will we return when we die?", indicated by what follows it, according to the reading of the majority. As for the second reading, the response of (idha) is omitted, that is: "we have returned"; it has been said: "that is a return." The meaning: their denial of resurrection after their death and their becoming dust.

Then they firmly judged their denial of resurrection, saying: "That, i.e., the resurrection, is ﴿a far-off return﴾," that is, far from the intellects, or the understandings, or the custom, or possibility. It is said: "I returned him, I return him, a returning," and "he returned, he returns, a return."

Then He, glorified be He, refuted what they said, saying: ﴿We certainly know what the earth diminishes of them﴾, that is, what it eats of their bodies, so nothing of that is lost to Us. And one whose knowledge encompasses everything, to the extent that it reaches the knowledge of what departs from the bodies of the dead in the graves, will not find resurrection difficult nor consider it far-fetched. al-Suddi said: "the diminishing here is death; He says: We know who dies among them and who remains, for whoever dies is buried, so it is as if the earth diminishes from the dead." It has also been said the meaning is: whoever among the polytheists enters Islam. The first is preferable. ﴿And with Us is a Book preserved﴾, that is, one that preserves their number and their names and everything among things; it is the Preserved Tablet, that is, guarded from the devils, or in which everything is preserved.

Then He, glorified be He, turned away from their first speech and moved to what is more heinous than it, saying: ﴿Nay, they denied the truth﴾, for it is an explicit statement from them of denial after what had preceded from them of mockery. The truth here means the Qur'an. al-Mawardi said: "according to all," and it has been said it is Islam, and it has been said it is Muhammad, and it has been said it is prophethood established by miracles. ﴿When it came to them﴾, that is, at the time of its coming to them, without reflection, without contemplation, and without close examination.

The majority read ﴿lamma﴾ with fatḥah on the lam and tashdid on the mim. al-Jahdari read it with kasrah on the lam and takhfif on the mim.

﴿So they are in a confused matter﴾, that is, mixed up and disturbed: they say at one time "sorcerer," at another "poet," and at another "soothsayer." Said by al-Zajjaj and others.

Qatadah said: "differing."

al-Hasan said: "confused." The meanings are close. It has been said: "corrupt," and the meanings are close.

From it is their saying: "the trusts of people became marij," i.e., corrupted, and "the religion and the matter marija," i.e., became mixed.

﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, that is: how did they neglect looking at the sky above them ﴿how We built it﴾ and made it in this description, raised without a pillar upon which it rests ﴿and adorned it﴾ with what We placed in it of lamps ﴿and it has no rifts﴾, that is, openings, cracks, and fissures. It is the plural of farj, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays: "He closes with it her gap from behind." al-Kisa'i said: "there is no disparity in it, no difference, and no openings."

﴿And the earth — We spread it out﴾, that is, We extended it, ﴿and cast into it firm mountains﴾, that is, stable mountains; the explanation of this has already passed in Surat al-Ra'd. ﴿And We caused to grow in it of every beautiful pair﴾, that is, of every good kind; the explanation of this has already passed in Surat al-Hajj.

﴿As an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back in repentance.﴾ These two are causes for what preceded, governed by the last verb of them, or by an implied one: that is, "We did what We did for insight and remembrance," as said by al-Zajjaj. Abu Hatim said: "they are in the accusative as verbal nouns (masdar), that is: We made that an insight and a reminder."

Al-Munib is the one who returns to Allah in repentance, who reflects upon the wonder of His creation and the marvels of His creatures.

In the context of this verse there is a reminder to those who deny resurrection, and an awakening for them from the course of heedlessness, and an explanation of the possibility of that and of its not being impossible, for whoever is capable of such matters is capable of it.

Likewise His saying: ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water﴾, that is, We sent down from the clouds water of abundant blessing, for people's benefit in most of their affairs. ﴿And We caused to grow by it gardens﴾, that is, We caused by that water many gardens to grow, ﴿and grain of the harvest﴾, that is, what is eaten as food and harvested of grains; the meaning is: the grain of the harvested crop, and the grain was singled out because it is the intended object. So said the Basrans. The Kufans said: it is from the genre of the attribution of a thing to itself, like "the congregational mosque," related by al-Farra'. al-Dahhak said: "the grain of the harvest is wheat and barley." It has been said: every grain that is harvested, stored, and eaten.

﴿And the tall palm trees, having fruit-clusters stacked one upon another﴾. It is coordinated with (gardens): that is, and We caused to grow by it the palm trees. Its singling out by mention, despite its inclusion among the gardens, is to indicate its excellence over the rest of the trees. The accusative of (bāsiqāt) is as a circumstantial state, and it is a presumed state, since at the time of growing they were not yet tall.

Mujahid, ʿIkrimah and Qatadah said: the bāsiqāt are the tall ones. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: "upright."

al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah and al-Farra' said: "heavy with fruit, pregnant," it is said of a she-goat when she bāsaqat: she gave birth. The more well-known in the language of the Arabs is the first. It is said: "the palm tree basaqat busuqan," when it grew tall. From it is the saying of the poet:

"For us is wine, but not the wine of a vineyard,
but from the produce of the tall palms,
noble in the sky, they have gone tall,
and their fruits have escaped the hands of the pickers."

The clause ﴿having fruit-clusters stacked one upon another﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial state of the palm trees. The ṭalʿ is the first thing that emerges from the fruit of the palm; it is said: "the ṭalʿ emerged, ṭuluʿan." The naḍīd is what is layered, one part stacked upon another, and that is before it opens; so it is naḍīd within its sheaths, and when it emerges from its sheaths it is no longer naḍīd.

﴿A provision for the servants﴾: its accusative is as a verbal noun, that is, "We provided them a provision," or as a reason, that is, "We caused these things to grow for provision." ﴿And We revived by it a dead land﴾, that is, We revived by that water a barren land having no fruit or crop. The clause ﴿Thus will be the emergence﴾ is a new sentence explaining that the emergence from the graves at the resurrection is like this revival by which Allah revived the dead earth.
