The *ba'* in *bil-wa'id* (with the threat) is extra for emphasis, or it is based on taking *qaddama* (sent forward) to mean *taqaddama* (went forward).

﴿The word is not changed before Me﴾. That is: there is no breaking of My promise; rather it is certain to occur, and I have decreed punishment upon you, so there is no altering of it. It has been said: this word is His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever brings an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 50, verse 16–35 (part 2 of 2):

It was said: it is His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ [Hud: 119]. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of the verse is that "the word is not altered in My presence by addition to it or subtraction from it, because of My knowledge of the unseen." This is the view of al-Kalbi, and al-Wahidi preferred it, because He said "with Me" (ladayya) and did not say "and My word is not changed." The first view is more preferable. It was also said: the object of ﴿I have already sent forth to you﴾ is ﴿the word is not altered﴾, i.e., "I have already sent forth to you this saying accompanied by the threat." This is very far-fetched. ﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾, i.e., I do not punish them unjustly, without a crime they committed or a sin they perpetrated. Since negating ẓallām (one who wrongs greatly) does not necessitate negating mere injustice (ẓulm), it was said that it here carries the meaning of ẓālim (wrongdoer), like tammār in the sense of tāmir (date-seller). It was also said: the intensive form is to emphasize this meaning by presenting the mentioned punishment without a sin in the context of exaggeration in injustice. It was also said: the intensive form is to observe the plurality of the servants, from the saying of people: "So-and-so is unjust to his servant" and "ẓallām to his servants." It was said other than this as well. The discussion of this has already passed in Surat Āl ʿImrān and Surat al-Ḥajj.

﴿On the Day when We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ Al-Jumhur read (naqūlu) with the nūn.
Nafi' and Abu Bakr read it with the yā'.
Al-Hasan read (aqūlu).
Al-A'mash read (yuqālu). The governing element of the adverbial phrase is ﴿what is changed of the word in My presence﴾, or it is elided, i.e., "remember" or "warn them." This speech is according to the manner of representation and imagination, and there is no question and no answer, so it was said; but the better view is that it is according to the manner of realization, and neither reason nor the Shariah prevents that.

Al-Wahidi said:
The exegetes said: Allah showed it the fulfillment of His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ [Hud: 119]. When it became filled, He said to it: ﴿Are you filled?﴾ and it says ﴿Is there any more?﴾, i.e., "I have been filled, and there remains in me no place that has not been filled."
This was said by ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid, and Muqātil ibn Sulaymān.
It was said: this interrogation carries the meaning of seeking more, i.e., it asks for an addition beyond those who have already entered it.
It was said: the meaning is that it asked that its size be increased because of its constriction by its people. The word al-mazīd is either a verbal noun like al-maḥīd, or a passive participle like al-manīʿ. The first means: "Is there any addition?" The second means: "Is there anything you can add to me?"

Then, when He finished explaining the state of the disbelievers, He began explaining the state of the believers, saying: ﴿And Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing, not far away﴾, i.e., Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing with a nearness that is not far, or a place not far from them, such that they see it at the place of standing, and look at what is in it, of which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. It is permissible that the accusative of ﴿not far away﴾ be in the state (ḥāl) position. (p-1401)

It was also said that the meaning is: it has adorned their hearts in this world with encouragement and warning, so it became near to their hearts. The first view is more preferable.

The reference in His saying ﴿This is what you were promised﴾ is to Paradise, with an implied verb: i.e., and it will be said to them, "This is what you were promised."
Al-Jumhur read (tūʿadūna) with the tā' (second-person).
Ibn Kathir read it with the yā' (third-person).
﴿For every returning penitent, observant﴾ is a substitute for ﴿for the God-fearing﴾ by repeating the preposition, or it is related to an elided verb that is in the state position: i.e., "said to them, for every returning penitent." The awwāb is the one who returns to Allah, the Exalted, in repentance from disobedience. It was said: he is the one who glorifies (Allah). It was said: he is the one who remembers Allah in solitude.
Al-Sha'bi and Mujahid said: he is the one who recalls his sins in solitude and then seeks forgiveness from Allah for them. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: he is the one who does not sit in a gathering until he seeks Allah's forgiveness in it. The ḥafīẓ (observant) is the one who guards his sins until he repents from them.
Qatadah said: he is the one who guards what Allah has entrusted him of His right and His blessing; this was also said by Mujahid.
It was said: he is the one who guards the command of Allah.
Al-Dahhak said: he is the one who guards Allah's commandment to him to accept.

﴿Who feared the Most Merciful in the unseen﴾ The relative clause is in the genitive position as a substitute or clarification of ﴿for every returning penitent﴾. It was said: it is permissible that it be a substitute after a substitute of "the God-fearing," but there is a problem with this, because a substitute and the thing it replaces should not be the same singular word repeated. It is also permissible that it be in the nominative position by way of resumption, with the predicate being ﴿enter it﴾, with the implied meaning: "it is said to them, enter it." Fearing in the unseen means to fear Allah while not having seen Him.
Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it means in seclusion, where no one sees him.
Al-Hasan said: when he draws the curtain and closes the door.
(The phrase "in the unseen") is related to an elided element that is in the state position, or an adjective of the verbal noun of khashiya (fear). ﴿And comes with a heart turning (in repentance)﴾, i.e., returning to Allah, sincere in obedience to Him. It was said: al-munīb is the one who turns to obedience. It was said: it is the sound one.
"Enter it" is with the implied verb: i.e., it is said to them, "Enter it." The plural is according to the meaning of "man" (min). I.e., enter Paradise in peace, meaning in safety from punishment. It was said: in peace from Allah and His angels. It was said: in safety from the cessation of blessings. This is related to an elided element in the state position: i.e., accompanied by peace. The reference in His saying ﴿That﴾ is to the time of that day, as Abu al-Baqa' said, and its predicate is ﴿the Day of Eternity﴾. He called it the Day of Eternity because it has no end; rather it is everlasting forever.

﴿For them is whatever they wish therein﴾, i.e., in Paradise is whatever their souls desire and their eyes delight in, of the varieties of blessings and kinds of good. ﴿And with Us is more﴾ of blessings which never occurred to their minds and never passed through their imagination.

Ibn Mardawayh has transmitted from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah descends upon the son of Adam in four stations: He is nearer to him than the jugular vein, He comes between a person and his heart, He holds the forelock of every creature, and He is with them wherever they are."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿the jugular vein﴾ that he said: the veins of the neck.
Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him that he said: it is the sinew of the heart.
Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, regarding His saying ﴿He does not utter a word except that with him is an watchful observer, ready﴾: he said: He records everything he says, good or evil, to the extent that he records his saying: "I ate, I drank, I went, I came, I saw." Then when Thursday comes, his saying and his deed are presented, and what was good or evil of it is confirmed, and the rest is discarded. That is His saying: ﴿Allah erases what He wills and establishes﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39].

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through the chain of ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: only good and evil are recorded; it does not record "O boy, saddle the horse" or "O boy, give me water."

It is established in the Two Sahihs and others from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah has forgiven this community what its souls speak of, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from ʿAmr ibn Dharr who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah is at the tongue of every speaker, so let a servant fear Allah and let him watch what he says."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), the like of it.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th, and Ibn ʿAsakir transmitted from ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan that he recited ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness﴾ and said: the driver drives it to the command of Allah, and the witness testifies against it for what it did.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th transmitted from Abu Hurayrah regarding the verse that he said: the driver is the angel, and the witness is the deed.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: the driver is from among the angels, and the witness is a witness against him from his own self.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him regarding ﴿You were certainly heedless of this﴾ that he said: it refers to the disbeliever.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him ﴿So We have removed from you your covering﴾, he said: it is life after death.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, and ﴿His companion will say﴾, he said: his devil.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim, regarding His saying ﴿Do not dispute before Me﴾, said: they offered excuses without a valid excuse, so Allah refuted their argument and rejected their saying.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾, he said: I do not punish one who has not committed a crime.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿On the Day when We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾, he said: "Is there any place in me that can be added to me?"

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others transmitted from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hell will continue to have people cast into it, and it will say, 'Is there any more?' until the Lord of Might places His foot in it, and then some of it will draw in upon others, and it will say: 'Enough, enough, by Your might and Your generosity.' And Paradise will continue to have surplus, until Allah creates for it another creation, and He will settle them in the surplus of Paradise."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim also transmitted a similar hadith from Abu Hurayrah, and there are other hadiths on this topic.

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿for every returning penitent, observant﴾, he said: he guarded his sins until he turned back from them.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa'l-Nushur transmitted from Anas, regarding His saying ﴿And with Us is more﴾, he said: (p-1402) the Lord, Blessed and Exalted, manifests Himself to them every Friday.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Ru'yah and al-Daylami transmitted from ʿAli regarding the verse that he said: the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, manifests Himself to them. There are other hadiths on this topic.

[p. 1399]

His words: ﴿Indeed, We created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him﴾. This is a new statement that contains a mention of part of God's power. By "man" is meant the species, though it has been said that it refers to Adam. Al-waswasah (whispering) is originally a faint sound, and here it means what stirs in his secret thoughts, his heart, and his inner self. That is, We know what he conceals and harbours within his soul. An example of using waswasah for a faint sound is the verse of al-A'sha:

*You hear the jingling of the anklets as she turns away*

So it was used for what is hidden in the speech of the soul. ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾. This is the vein of the shoulder, which extends from the side of his throat to his shoulder. These are two veins, one on the right and one on the left.

Al-Hasan said: al-Warid is al-Watain (the aorta), which is a vessel attached to the heart.

This is an illustration of nearness by the nearness of that vessel to the human being. That is: We are nearer to him than the vein of his jugular. The construction is explanatory (idafah bayaniyyah, a construction in which the second noun specifies the first): that is, a vein which is the warid.

It has been said that al-habl (the vein) is the same as al-warid, so it is like masjid al-jami' (the congregational mosque).

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned that, along with His knowledge of it, He has appointed for him two angels who record and preserve his deeds against him, as a means of establishing the proof. So He said: ﴿When the two receivers receive﴾. The adverbial phrase *idh* (when) is governed by the sense of the verb contained in *aqrab* (nearer). It is also permissible for it to be governed by an implied verb, *udhkur* (mention). The meaning is: He is nearer to him than the vein of his jugular when the two receivers receive. They are the two angels appointed over him, for whatever he utters and whatever he does. That is, they take that down and record it.

*Al-talaqqi* means taking. That is: We are most knowing of his circumstances, not needing the guardians appointed over him.

We made that as a means of establishing the proof and of emphasising the matter.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Mujahid said: "The two receivers are two angels who receive your deeds, one of them on your right, recording your good deeds, and the other on your left, recording your evil deeds."

Mujahid also said: God has appointed for the human being two angels by night and two by day, who guard his deeds and record their effects. ﴿On the right and on the left, one seated﴾. He said *qa'id* (seated) and did not say *qa'idan* (two seated), though they are two, because the meaning is: on the right, a seated one, and on the left, a seated one. So the first was omitted because the second indicates it. This is what Sibawayh said, like the words of the poet:

*We are with what we have, and you are with what you have, content, though the opinion differs.*

And the words of al-Farazdaq:

*And he came, and he was, and I was, not one to excuse.*

That is: "and he was not one to excuse, and I was not one to excuse." Al-Akhfash and al-Farra' said: the word *qa'id* is suitable for the singular, the dual and the plural, and needs no implied element in the first case.

Al-Jawhari and others among the imams of language and grammar said: *fa'il* and *fa'ul* are forms in which the singular, the dual and the plural are alike. *Al-qa'id* means one who sits, like *al-jalis* in the sense of *al-mujalis* (companion).

﴿He does not utter a word but there is with him a watchful observer, ready﴾. That is: he does not speak any speech, uttering it and casting it from his mouth, but with the one who utters it there is a watcher. That is: an angel who watches his words and records them. *Al-raqib* (watcher) is the one who preserves and follows the affairs of the human being, who records what he says of good and evil.

So the recorder of good is the angel of the right, and the recorder of evil is the angel of the left.

*Al-'atid* is the present and prepared one. Al-Jawhari said: *al-'atid* is the present and prepared one. It is said: *'attadahu ta'tidan* and *a'taddahu i'tidadan*, that is, he prepared it. From this is the verse ﴿and she prepared for them a couch﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. What is meant here is that he is made ready for writing and prepared for it.

﴿And the agony of death has come in truth﴾. When He, glorified is He, made clear that all his deeds are preserved and recorded, He mentioned after it what befalls them of death. By *sakratu al-mawt* (the agony of death) is meant its severity and its overwhelming, which covers the human being and overcomes his reason. The meaning of *bi'l-haqq* (in truth) is that at death the truth becomes clear to him, and the truthfulness of what the messengers brought of reports about resurrection, promise and threat becomes manifest to him. It has been said: the truth is death. It has also been said that there is inversion in the speech: that is, "the agony of the truth has come with death." Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Ibn Mas'ud also read it this way.

*Al-sakrah* is the truth, and it is attributed to itself because the two wordings differ. It has been said that the *ba'* (with) is for accompaniment, as in His words ﴿grows with oil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20]. That is: accompanied by the truth, that is, by the reality of the situation. The indication in His words *dhalika* (that) refers to death. *Al-hayd* is inclination. That is: that death, from which you used to incline and flee. It is said: *hada 'an al-shay'* yahidu huyudan, hayduda and hidah, meaning he inclined from it and turned aside. From this is the words of Tarafah:

*O Abu Munthir, you desired fidelity, so you feared it, and you swerved as the camel swerves from the slippery ground.*

Al-Hasan said: *tahid* means *tahrub* (flees).

﴿And the Trumpet is blown﴾. He expressed it in the past tense because its occurrence is certain. This is the final blast for resurrection. ﴿That is the Day of the Threat﴾. That is: that time, in which the blowing of the Trumpet occurs, is the Day of the Threat which God threatened the disbelievers with.

Muqatil said: by the threat is meant the punishment in the Hereafter. He singled out the threat, although the day is both the Day of Promise and of Threat, to magnify its terror.

﴿And every soul comes, with it a driver and a witness﴾. That is: every soul of the souls comes with someone who drives it and someone who bears witness for it or against it.

They differed about the driver and the witness. Al-Dahhak said: the driver is from among the angels, and the witness is from among themselves: that is, their hands and feet.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: a driver who drives it, and a witness who bears witness against it for its deeds.

Ibn Muslim said: the driver is its companion from among the devils; he is called a driver because he follows it, even if he does not urge it on.

Mujahid said: the driver and the witness are two angels.

It has been said: the driver is the angel, and the witness is the deed. It has been said: the driver is the recorder of evil deeds, and the witness is the recorder of good deeds. The clause occupies the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿You were heedless of this﴾. That is, it will be said to him: "You were heedless of this." The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from *nafs* (soul), or it is a new clause, as if it were said: "what is said to him."

Al-Dahhak said: by "this" is meant the polytheists, because they were heedless of the consequences of their affairs.

Ibn Zayd said: the address is to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): that is, "You were, O Muhammad, heedless of the message."

Most of the commentators said: what is meant is all creation, the righteous and the wicked among them, and Ibn Jarir chose this view.

The majority read *kunta* with a *fatha* on the *ta'* and *ghita'aka* and *basaruka* with a *fatha* on the *kaf*, in accordance with the masculine wording of *kull* (every).

Al-Jahdari and Talhah ibn Musarrif read with a *kasrah* throughout, on the basis that what is meant is the soul (nafs, feminine).

﴿So We have removed from you your covering﴾, which was in the world. That is: We removed the veil that was between you and the affairs of the Hereafter, and removed your heedlessness of that. ﴿So your sight today is sharp﴾. That is: penetrating, by which you see what was hidden from you of the world.

Al-Suddi said: by the covering is meant that he was in his mother's womb and then was born. It has been said that he was in the grave and then was raised. The first is preferable.

As for *al-basar* (sight), it has been said it is the sight of the heart, and it has been said it is the sight of the eye.

Mujahid said: your sight is directed at the tongue of your scale when your good and evil deeds are weighed. Al-Dahhak also said this.

﴿And his companion says: "This is what I have ready"﴾. That is: the angel appointed over him says: "This is what I have from the book of your deeds, ready, present, which I have prepared." So said al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

Mujahid said: the angel says to the Lord, glorified is He: "This is the one You appointed me over from the children of Adam; I have brought him and brought the register of his deeds."

It is related from him that he said: his companion is from the devils, and he says this: that is, "This is what I have prepared for you by my seduction and misguidance."

Ibn Zayd said: what is meant here is his companion from mankind. *'Atid* is in the nominative case as an attribute of *ma* (what), if it is a qualified noun; if it is a relative, it is a predicate after a predicate, or the predicate of an implied subject.

﴿Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever﴾. This is an address from God, mighty and majestic, to the driver and the witness.

Al-Zajjaj said: this is a command to the two angels appointed over him, who are the driver and the witness: "every disbeliever in blessings, stubborn, turning away from faith."

﴿Hindering the good﴾, not spending any good; ﴿transgressing, a doubter﴾, one who does not acknowledge the unity of God; ﴿doubting﴾, uncertain about the truth, from their saying *arāba al-rajul*, when a man became one who has doubt.

It has been said: this is an address to the two angels of the guards of the Fire.

It has been said: this is an address to one person, with the dual of the agent being treated as the dual of the verb and its repetition.

Al-Khalil and al-Akhfash said: this is the correct usage of the Arabs, that a single person is addressed with the dual form. They say *irhalaha*, *izjuraha*, *khudhahu*, *atliqahu*, to a single person.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say to a single person *quma 'anna* (stand away from us).

The origin of this is that the least of a man's helpers with his camels, sheep and companions on a journey are two. So the speech of a man to one person proceeded in accordance with that. From it is the saying of the Arabs to one person in poetry, as Imru' al-Qays said:

*O my two friends, pass by me over Umm Jundab, so we may soothe the bindings of the tormented heart.*

And his words:

*Stop, let us weep for the memory of a beloved and a dwelling, at the edge of al-Liwa, between al-Dukhul and Hawmal.*

And the words of another:

*If you two rebuke me, O son of Affan, I will be rebuked; and if you two call me, I will protect an honour that is defended.*

Al-Mazini said: His words *alqiya* (cast, dual) indicate *alqi alqi* (cast, cast). Al-Mubarrad said: it is a dual for emphasis, so *alqiya* stands in place of *alqi alqi*.

Mujahid and Ikrimah said: *al-'anid* is the one who opposes the truth. It has been said: the one who turns away from the truth. It is said: *'anada ya'nidu* with *kasrah*, *'unudan*, when he opposed the truth.

﴿Who set up with God another god﴾. It may be a substitute for *kull* (every), or an accusative in dispraise, or a substitute for *kaffar* (disbeliever), or nominative as a subject, or the predicate. ﴿So cast him into the severe punishment﴾. This is an emphasis of the first command, or a substitute for it.

﴿His companion says: "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress; but he was in far-off error"﴾. This clause is a new statement explaining what the companion says. By the companion here is meant the devil who was assigned to this disbeliever. He denied that he had caused him to transgress. Then he said: ﴿but he was in far-off error﴾: that is, far from the truth; so I called him and he responded to me; had he been one of Your sincere servants, I would not have been able to overcome him. It has been said that his companion is the angel who used to record his evil deeds, and that the disbeliever says: "Lord, he hastened me," and He answers him with this. Thus said Muqatil and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The first is preferable, and the majority held it.

﴿He says: "Do not dispute before Me"﴾. This clause is a new statement answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did God say?" So it is said: ﴿He says: "Do not dispute before Me"﴾, meaning the disbelievers and their companions. He, glorified is He, forbade them to dispute at the place of reckoning. The clause ﴿and I had already sent to you the threat﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, while the situation is that I had already sent to you the threat by sending the messengers and revealing the books. The *ba'* in *bil-wa'id* (with the threat) is extra for emphasis, or it is based on taking *qaddama* (sent forward) to mean *taqaddama* (went forward).

﴿The word is not changed before Me﴾. That is: there is no breaking of My promise; rather it is certain to occur, and I have decreed punishment upon you, so there is no altering of it. It has been said: this word is His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever brings an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 50, verse 16–35 (part 2 of 2):

It was said: it is His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ [Hud: 119]. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of the verse is that "the word is not altered in My presence by addition to it or subtraction from it, because of My knowledge of the unseen." This is the view of al-Kalbi, and al-Wahidi preferred it, because He said "with Me" (ladayya) and did not say "and My word is not changed." The first view is more preferable. It was also said: the object of ﴿I have already sent forth to you﴾ is ﴿the word is not altered﴾, i.e., "I have already sent forth to you this saying accompanied by the threat." This is very far-fetched. ﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾, i.e., I do not punish them unjustly, without a crime they committed or a sin they perpetrated. Since negating ẓallām (one who wrongs greatly) does not necessitate negating mere injustice (ẓulm), it was said that it here carries the meaning of ẓālim (wrongdoer), like tammār in the sense of tāmir (date-seller). It was also said: the intensive form is to emphasize this meaning by presenting the mentioned punishment without a sin in the context of exaggeration in injustice. It was also said: the intensive form is to observe the plurality of the servants, from the saying of people: "So-and-so is unjust to his servant" and "ẓallām to his servants." It was said other than this as well. The discussion of this has already passed in Surat Āl ʿImrān and Surat al-Ḥajj.

﴿On the Day when We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ Al-Jumhur read (naqūlu) with the nūn.
Nafi' and Abu Bakr read it with the yā'.
Al-Hasan read (aqūlu).
Al-A'mash read (yuqālu). The governing element of the adverbial phrase is ﴿what is changed of the word in My presence﴾, or it is elided, i.e., "remember" or "warn them." This speech is according to the manner of representation and imagination, and there is no question and no answer, so it was said; but the better view is that it is according to the manner of realization, and neither reason nor the Shariah prevents that.

Al-Wahidi said:
The exegetes said: Allah showed it the fulfillment of His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ [Hud: 119]. When it became filled, He said to it: ﴿Are you filled?﴾ and it says ﴿Is there any more?﴾, i.e., "I have been filled, and there remains in me no place that has not been filled."
This was said by ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid, and Muqātil ibn Sulaymān.
It was said: this interrogation carries the meaning of seeking more, i.e., it asks for an addition beyond those who have already entered it.
It was said: the meaning is that it asked that its size be increased because of its constriction by its people. The word al-mazīd is either a verbal noun like al-maḥīd, or a passive participle like al-manīʿ. The first means: "Is there any addition?" The second means: "Is there anything you can add to me?"

Then, when He finished explaining the state of the disbelievers, He began explaining the state of the believers, saying: ﴿And Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing, not far away﴾, i.e., Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing with a nearness that is not far, or a place not far from them, such that they see it at the place of standing, and look at what is in it, of which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. It is permissible that the accusative of ﴿not far away﴾ be in the state (ḥāl) position. (p-1401)

It was also said that the meaning is: it has adorned their hearts in this world with encouragement and warning, so it became near to their hearts. The first view is more preferable.

The reference in His saying ﴿This is what you were promised﴾ is to Paradise, with an implied verb: i.e., and it will be said to them, "This is what you were promised."
Al-Jumhur read (tūʿadūna) with the tā' (second-person).
Ibn Kathir read it with the yā' (third-person).
﴿For every returning penitent, observant﴾ is a substitute for ﴿for the God-fearing﴾ by repeating the preposition, or it is related to an elided verb that is in the state position: i.e., "said to them, for every returning penitent." The awwāb is the one who returns to Allah, the Exalted, in repentance from disobedience. It was said: he is the one who glorifies (Allah). It was said: he is the one who remembers Allah in solitude.
Al-Sha'bi and Mujahid said: he is the one who recalls his sins in solitude and then seeks forgiveness from Allah for them. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: he is the one who does not sit in a gathering until he seeks Allah's forgiveness in it. The ḥafīẓ (observant) is the one who guards his sins until he repents from them.
Qatadah said: he is the one who guards what Allah has entrusted him of His right and His blessing; this was also said by Mujahid.
It was said: he is the one who guards the command of Allah.
Al-Dahhak said: he is the one who guards Allah's commandment to him to accept.

﴿Who feared the Most Merciful in the unseen﴾ The relative clause is in the genitive position as a substitute or clarification of ﴿for every returning penitent﴾. It was said: it is permissible that it be a substitute after a substitute of "the God-fearing," but there is a problem with this, because a substitute and the thing it replaces should not be the same singular word repeated. It is also permissible that it be in the nominative position by way of resumption, with the predicate being ﴿enter it﴾, with the implied meaning: "it is said to them, enter it." Fearing in the unseen means to fear Allah while not having seen Him.
Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it means in seclusion, where no one sees him.
Al-Hasan said: when he draws the curtain and closes the door.
(The phrase "in the unseen") is related to an elided element that is in the state position, or an adjective of the verbal noun of khashiya (fear). ﴿And comes with a heart turning (in repentance)﴾, i.e., returning to Allah, sincere in obedience to Him. It was said: al-munīb is the one who turns to obedience. It was said: it is the sound one.
"Enter it" is with the implied verb: i.e., it is said to them, "Enter it." The plural is according to the meaning of "man" (min). I.e., enter Paradise in peace, meaning in safety from punishment. It was said: in peace from Allah and His angels. It was said: in safety from the cessation of blessings. This is related to an elided element in the state position: i.e., accompanied by peace. The reference in His saying ﴿That﴾ is to the time of that day, as Abu al-Baqa' said, and its predicate is ﴿the Day of Eternity﴾. He called it the Day of Eternity because it has no end; rather it is everlasting forever.

﴿For them is whatever they wish therein﴾, i.e., in Paradise is whatever their souls desire and their eyes delight in, of the varieties of blessings and kinds of good. ﴿And with Us is more﴾ of blessings which never occurred to their minds and never passed through their imagination.

Ibn Mardawayh has transmitted from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah descends upon the son of Adam in four stations: He is nearer to him than the jugular vein, He comes between a person and his heart, He holds the forelock of every creature, and He is with them wherever they are."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿the jugular vein﴾ that he said: the veins of the neck.
Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him that he said: it is the sinew of the heart.
Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, regarding His saying ﴿He does not utter a word except that with him is an watchful observer, ready﴾: he said: He records everything he says, good or evil, to the extent that he records his saying: "I ate, I drank, I went, I came, I saw." Then when Thursday comes, his saying and his deed are presented, and what was good or evil of it is confirmed, and the rest is discarded. That is His saying: ﴿Allah erases what He wills and establishes﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39].

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through the chain of ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: only good and evil are recorded; it does not record "O boy, saddle the horse" or "O boy, give me water."

It is established in the Two Sahihs and others from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah has forgiven this community what its souls speak of, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from ʿAmr ibn Dharr who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah is at the tongue of every speaker, so let a servant fear Allah and let him watch what he says."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), the like of it.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th, and Ibn ʿAsakir transmitted from ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan that he recited ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness﴾ and said: the driver drives it to the command of Allah, and the witness testifies against it for what it did.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th transmitted from Abu Hurayrah regarding the verse that he said: the driver is the angel, and the witness is the deed.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: the driver is from among the angels, and the witness is a witness against him from his own self.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him regarding ﴿You were certainly heedless of this﴾ that he said: it refers to the disbeliever.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him ﴿So We have removed from you your covering﴾, he said: it is life after death.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, and ﴿His companion will say﴾, he said: his devil.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim, regarding His saying ﴿Do not dispute before Me﴾, said: they offered excuses without a valid excuse, so Allah refuted their argument and rejected their saying.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾, he said: I do not punish one who has not committed a crime.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿On the Day when We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾, he said: "Is there any place in me that can be added to me?"

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others transmitted from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hell will continue to have people cast into it, and it will say, 'Is there any more?' until the Lord of Might places His foot in it, and then some of it will draw in upon others, and it will say: 'Enough, enough, by Your might and Your generosity.' And Paradise will continue to have surplus, until Allah creates for it another creation, and He will settle them in the surplus of Paradise."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim also transmitted a similar hadith from Abu Hurayrah, and there are other hadiths on this topic.

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿for every returning penitent, observant﴾, he said: he guarded his sins until he turned back from them.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa'l-Nushur transmitted from Anas, regarding His saying ﴿And with Us is more﴾, he said: (p-1402) the Lord, Blessed and Exalted, manifests Himself to them every Friday.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Ru'yah and al-Daylami transmitted from ʿAli regarding the verse that he said: the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, manifests Himself to them. There are other hadiths on this topic.

[p. 1399]

His words: ﴿Indeed, We created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him﴾. This is a new statement that contains a mention of part of God's power. By "man" is meant the species, though it has been said that it refers to Adam. Al-waswasah (whispering) is originally a faint sound, and here it means what stirs in his secret thoughts, his heart, and his inner self. That is, We know what he conceals and harbours within his soul. An example of using waswasah for a faint sound is the verse of al-A'sha:

*You hear the jingling of the anklets as she turns away*

So it was used for what is hidden in the speech of the soul. ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾. This is the vein of the shoulder, which extends from the side of his throat to his shoulder. These are two veins, one on the right and one on the left.

Al-Hasan said: al-Warid is al-Watain (the aorta), which is a vessel attached to the heart.

This is an illustration of nearness by the nearness of that vessel to the human being. That is: We are nearer to him than the vein of his jugular. The construction is explanatory (idafah bayaniyyah, a construction in which the second noun specifies the first): that is, a vein which is the warid.

It has been said that al-habl (the vein) is the same as al-warid, so it is like masjid al-jami' (the congregational mosque).

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned that, along with His knowledge of it, He has appointed for him two angels who record and preserve his deeds against him, as a means of establishing the proof. So He said: ﴿When the two receivers receive﴾. The adverbial phrase *idh* (when) is governed by the sense of the verb contained in *aqrab* (nearer). It is also permissible for it to be governed by an implied verb, *udhkur* (mention). The meaning is: He is nearer to him than the vein of his jugular when the two receivers receive. They are the two angels appointed over him, for whatever he utters and whatever he does. That is, they take that down and record it.

*Al-talaqqi* means taking. That is: We are most knowing of his circumstances, not needing the guardians appointed over him.

We made that as a means of establishing the proof and of emphasising the matter.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Mujahid said: "The two receivers are two angels who receive your deeds, one of them on your right, recording your good deeds, and the other on your left, recording your evil deeds."

Mujahid also said: God has appointed for the human being two angels by night and two by day, who guard his deeds and record their effects. ﴿On the right and on the left, one seated﴾. He said *qa'id* (seated) and did not say *qa'idan* (two seated), though they are two, because the meaning is: on the right, a seated one, and on the left, a seated one. So the first was omitted because the second indicates it. This is what Sibawayh said, like the words of the poet:

*We are with what we have, and you are with what you have, content, though the opinion differs.*

And the words of al-Farazdaq:

*And he came, and he was, and I was, not one to excuse.*

That is: "and he was not one to excuse, and I was not one to excuse." Al-Akhfash and al-Farra' said: the word *qa'id* is suitable for the singular, the dual and the plural, and needs no implied element in the first case.

Al-Jawhari and others among the imams of language and grammar said: *fa'il* and *fa'ul* are forms in which the singular, the dual and the plural are alike. *Al-qa'id* means one who sits, like *al-jalis* in the sense of *al-mujalis* (companion).

﴿He does not utter a word but there is with him a watchful observer, ready﴾. That is: he does not speak any speech, uttering it and casting it from his mouth, but with the one who utters it there is a watcher. That is: an angel who watches his words and records them. *Al-raqib* (watcher) is the one who preserves and follows the affairs of the human being, who records what he says of good and evil.

So the recorder of good is the angel of the right, and the recorder of evil is the angel of the left.

*Al-'atid* is the present and prepared one. Al-Jawhari said: *al-'atid* is the present and prepared one. It is said: *'attadahu ta'tidan* and *a'taddahu i'tidadan*, that is, he prepared it. From this is the verse ﴿and she prepared for them a couch﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. What is meant here is that he is made ready for writing and prepared for it.

﴿And the agony of death has come in truth﴾. When He, glorified is He, made clear that all his deeds are preserved and recorded, He mentioned after it what befalls them of death. By *sakratu al-mawt* (the agony of death) is meant its severity and its overwhelming, which covers the human being and overcomes his reason. The meaning of *bi'l-haqq* (in truth) is that at death the truth becomes clear to him, and the truthfulness of what the messengers brought of reports about resurrection, promise and threat becomes manifest to him. It has been said: the truth is death. It has also been said that there is inversion in the speech: that is, "the agony of the truth has come with death." Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Ibn Mas'ud also read it this way.

*Al-sakrah* is the truth, and it is attributed to itself because the two wordings differ. It has been said that the *ba'* (with) is for accompaniment, as in His words ﴿grows with oil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20]. That is: accompanied by the truth, that is, by the reality of the situation. The indication in His words *dhalika* (that) refers to death. *Al-hayd* is inclination. That is: that death, from which you used to incline and flee. It is said: *hada 'an al-shay'* yahidu huyudan, hayduda and hidah, meaning he inclined from it and turned aside. From this is the words of Tarafah:

*O Abu Munthir, you desired fidelity, so you feared it, and you swerved as the camel swerves from the slippery ground.*

Al-Hasan said: *tahid* means *tahrub* (flees).

﴿And the Trumpet is blown﴾. He expressed it in the past tense because its occurrence is certain. This is the final blast for resurrection. ﴿That is the Day of the Threat﴾. That is: that time, in which the blowing of the Trumpet occurs, is the Day of the Threat which God threatened the disbelievers with.

Muqatil said: by the threat is meant the punishment in the Hereafter. He singled out the threat, although the day is both the Day of Promise and of Threat, to magnify its terror.

﴿And every soul comes, with it a driver and a witness﴾. That is: every soul of the souls comes with someone who drives it and someone who bears witness for it or against it.

They differed about the driver and the witness. Al-Dahhak said: the driver is from among the angels, and the witness is from among themselves: that is, their hands and feet.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: a driver who drives it, and a witness who bears witness against it for its deeds.

Ibn Muslim said: the driver is its companion from among the devils; he is called a driver because he follows it, even if he does not urge it on.

Mujahid said: the driver and the witness are two angels.

It has been said: the driver is the angel, and the witness is the deed. It has been said: the driver is the recorder of evil deeds, and the witness is the recorder of good deeds. The clause occupies the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿You were heedless of this﴾. That is, it will be said to him: "You were heedless of this." The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from *nafs* (soul), or it is a new clause, as if it were said: "what is said to him."

Al-Dahhak said: by "this" is meant the polytheists, because they were heedless of the consequences of their affairs.

Ibn Zayd said: the address is to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): that is, "You were, O Muhammad, heedless of the message."

Most of the commentators said: what is meant is all creation, the righteous and the wicked among them, and Ibn Jarir chose this view.

The majority read *kunta* with a *fatha* on the *ta'* and *ghita'aka* and *basaruka* with a *fatha* on the *kaf*, in accordance with the masculine wording of *kull* (every).

Al-Jahdari and Talhah ibn Musarrif read with a *kasrah* throughout, on the basis that what is meant is the soul (nafs, feminine).

﴿So We have removed from you your covering﴾, which was in the world. That is: We removed the veil that was between you and the affairs of the Hereafter, and removed your heedlessness of that. ﴿So your sight today is sharp﴾. That is: penetrating, by which you see what was hidden from you of the world.

Al-Suddi said: by the covering is meant that he was in his mother's womb and then was born. It has been said that he was in the grave and then was raised. The first is preferable.

As for *al-basar* (sight), it has been said it is the sight of the heart, and it has been said it is the sight of the eye.

Mujahid said: your sight is directed at the tongue of your scale when your good and evil deeds are weighed. Al-Dahhak also said this.

﴿And his companion says: "This is what I have ready"﴾. That is: the angel appointed over him says: "This is what I have from the book of your deeds, ready, present, which I have prepared." So said al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

Mujahid said: the angel says to the Lord, glorified is He: "This is the one You appointed me over from the children of Adam; I have brought him and brought the register of his deeds."

It is related from him that he said: his companion is from the devils, and he says this: that is, "This is what I have prepared for you by my seduction and misguidance."

Ibn Zayd said: what is meant here is his companion from mankind. *'Atid* is in the nominative case as an attribute of *ma* (what), if it is a qualified noun; if it is a relative, it is a predicate after a predicate, or the predicate of an implied subject.

﴿Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever﴾. This is an address from God, mighty and majestic, to the driver and the witness.

Al-Zajjaj said: this is a command to the two angels appointed over him, who are the driver and the witness: "every disbeliever in blessings, stubborn, turning away from faith."

﴿Hindering the good﴾, not spending any good; ﴿transgressing, a doubter﴾, one who does not acknowledge the unity of God; ﴿doubting﴾, uncertain about the truth, from their saying *arāba al-rajul*, when a man became one who has doubt.

It has been said: this is an address to the two angels of the guards of the Fire.

It has been said: this is an address to one person, with the dual of the agent being treated as the dual of the verb and its repetition.

Al-Khalil and al-Akhfash said: this is the correct usage of the Arabs, that a single person is addressed with the dual form. They say *irhalaha*, *izjuraha*, *khudhahu*, *atliqahu*, to a single person.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say to a single person *quma 'anna* (stand away from us).

The origin of this is that the least of a man's helpers with his camels, sheep and companions on a journey are two. So the speech of a man to one person proceeded in accordance with that. From it is the saying of the Arabs to one person in poetry, as Imru' al-Qays said:

*O my two friends, pass by me over Umm Jundab, so we may soothe the bindings of the tormented heart.*

And his words:

*Stop, let us weep for the memory of a beloved and a dwelling, at the edge of al-Liwa, between al-Dukhul and Hawmal.*

And the words of another:

*If you two rebuke me, O son of Affan, I will be rebuked; and if you two call me, I will protect an honour that is defended.*

Al-Mazini said: His words *alqiya* (cast, dual) indicate *alqi alqi* (cast, cast). Al-Mubarrad said: it is a dual for emphasis, so *alqiya* stands in place of *alqi alqi*.

Mujahid and Ikrimah said: *al-'anid* is the one who opposes the truth. It has been said: the one who turns away from the truth. It is said: *'anada ya'nidu* with *kasrah*, *'unudan*, when he opposed the truth.

﴿Who set up with God another god﴾. It may be a substitute for *kull* (every), or an accusative in dispraise, or a substitute for *kaffar* (disbeliever), or nominative as a subject, or the predicate. ﴿So cast him into the severe punishment﴾. This is an emphasis of the first command, or a substitute for it.

﴿His companion says: "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress; but he was in far-off error"﴾. This clause is a new statement explaining what the companion says. By the companion here is meant the devil who was assigned to this disbeliever. He denied that he had caused him to transgress. Then he said: ﴿but he was in far-off error﴾: that is, far from the truth; so I called him and he responded to me; had he been one of Your sincere servants, I would not have been able to overcome him. It has been said that his companion is the angel who used to record his evil deeds, and that the disbeliever says: "Lord, he hastened me," and He answers him with this. Thus said Muqatil and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The first is preferable, and the majority held it.

﴿He says: "Do not dispute before Me"﴾. This clause is a new statement answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did God say?" So it is said: ﴿He says: "Do not dispute before Me"﴾, meaning the disbelievers and their companions. He, glorified is He, forbade them to dispute at the place of reckoning. The clause ﴿and I had already sent to you the threat﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, while the situation is that I had already sent to you the threat by sending the messengers and revealing the books. The *ba'* in *bil-wa'id* (with the threat) is extra for emphasis, or it is based on taking *qaddama* (sent forward) to mean *taqaddama* (went forward).

﴿The word is not changed before Me﴾. That is: there is no breaking of My promise; rather it is certain to occur, and I have decreed punishment upon you, so there is no altering of it. It has been said: this word is His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever brings an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 50, verse 16–35 (part 2 of 2):

It was said: it is His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ [Hud: 119]. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of the verse is that "the word is not altered in My presence by addition to it or subtraction from it, because of My knowledge of the unseen." This is the view of al-Kalbi, and al-Wahidi preferred it, because He said "with Me" (ladayya) and did not say "and My word is not changed." The first view is more preferable. It was also said: the object of ﴿I have already sent forth to you﴾ is ﴿the word is not altered﴾, i.e., "I have already sent forth to you this saying accompanied by the threat." This is very far-fetched. ﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾, i.e., I do not punish them unjustly, without a crime they committed or a sin they perpetrated. Since negating ẓallām (one who wrongs greatly) does not necessitate negating mere injustice (ẓulm), it was said that it here carries the meaning of ẓālim (wrongdoer), like tammār in the sense of tāmir (date-seller). It was also said: the intensive form is to emphasize this meaning by presenting the mentioned punishment without a sin in the context of exaggeration in injustice. It was also said: the intensive form is to observe the plurality of the servants, from the saying of people: "So-and-so is unjust to his servant" and "ẓallām to his servants." It was said other than this as well. The discussion of this has already passed in Surat Āl ʿImrān and Surat al-Ḥajj.

﴿On the Day when We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ Al-Jumhur read (naqūlu) with the nūn.
Nafi' and Abu Bakr read it with the yā'.
Al-Hasan read (aqūlu).
Al-A'mash read (yuqālu). The governing element of the adverbial phrase is ﴿what is changed of the word in My presence﴾, or it is elided, i.e., "remember" or "warn them." This speech is according to the manner of representation and imagination, and there is no question and no answer, so it was said; but the better view is that it is according to the manner of realization, and neither reason nor the Shariah prevents that.

Al-Wahidi said:
The exegetes said: Allah showed it the fulfillment of His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ [Hud: 119]. When it became filled, He said to it: ﴿Are you filled?﴾ and it says ﴿Is there any more?﴾, i.e., "I have been filled, and there remains in me no place that has not been filled."
This was said by ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid, and Muqātil ibn Sulaymān.
It was said: this interrogation carries the meaning of seeking more, i.e., it asks for an addition beyond those who have already entered it.
It was said: the meaning is that it asked that its size be increased because of its constriction by its people. The word al-mazīd is either a verbal noun like al-maḥīd, or a passive participle like al-manīʿ. The first means: "Is there any addition?" The second means: "Is there anything you can add to me?"

Then, when He finished explaining the state of the disbelievers, He began explaining the state of the believers, saying: ﴿And Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing, not far away﴾, i.e., Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing with a nearness that is not far, or a place not far from them, such that they see it at the place of standing, and look at what is in it, of which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. It is permissible that the accusative of ﴿not far away﴾ be in the state (ḥāl) position. (p-1401)

It was also said that the meaning is: it has adorned their hearts in this world with encouragement and warning, so it became near to their hearts. The first view is more preferable.

The reference in His saying ﴿This is what you were promised﴾ is to Paradise, with an implied verb: i.e., and it will be said to them, "This is what you were promised."
Al-Jumhur read (tūʿadūna) with the tā' (second-person).
Ibn Kathir read it with the yā' (third-person).
﴿For every returning penitent, observant﴾ is a substitute for ﴿for the God-fearing﴾ by repeating the preposition, or it is related to an elided verb that is in the state position: i.e., "said to them, for every returning penitent." The awwāb is the one who returns to Allah, the Exalted, in repentance from disobedience. It was said: he is the one who glorifies (Allah). It was said: he is the one who remembers Allah in solitude.
Al-Sha'bi and Mujahid said: he is the one who recalls his sins in solitude and then seeks forgiveness from Allah for them. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: he is the one who does not sit in a gathering until he seeks Allah's forgiveness in it. The ḥafīẓ (observant) is the one who guards his sins until he repents from them.
Qatadah said: he is the one who guards what Allah has entrusted him of His right and His blessing; this was also said by Mujahid.
It was said: he is the one who guards the command of Allah.
Al-Dahhak said: he is the one who guards Allah's commandment to him to accept.

﴿Who feared the Most Merciful in the unseen﴾ The relative clause is in the genitive position as a substitute or clarification of ﴿for every returning penitent﴾. It was said: it is permissible that it be a substitute after a substitute of "the God-fearing," but there is a problem with this, because a substitute and the thing it replaces should not be the same singular word repeated. It is also permissible that it be in the nominative position by way of resumption, with the predicate being ﴿enter it﴾, with the implied meaning: "it is said to them, enter it." Fearing in the unseen means to fear Allah while not having seen Him.
Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it means in seclusion, where no one sees him.
Al-Hasan said: when he draws the curtain and closes the door.
(The phrase "in the unseen") is related to an elided element that is in the state position, or an adjective of the verbal noun of khashiya (fear). ﴿And comes with a heart turning (in repentance)﴾, i.e., returning to Allah, sincere in obedience to Him. It was said: al-munīb is the one who turns to obedience. It was said: it is the sound one.
"Enter it" is with the implied verb: i.e., it is said to them, "Enter it." The plural is according to the meaning of "man" (min). I.e., enter Paradise in peace, meaning in safety from punishment. It was said: in peace from Allah and His angels. It was said: in safety from the cessation of blessings. This is related to an elided element in the state position: i.e., accompanied by peace. The reference in His saying ﴿That﴾ is to the time of that day, as Abu al-Baqa' said, and its predicate is ﴿the Day of Eternity﴾. He called it the Day of Eternity because it has no end; rather it is everlasting forever.

﴿For them is whatever they wish therein﴾, i.e., in Paradise is whatever their souls desire and their eyes delight in, of the varieties of blessings and kinds of good. ﴿And with Us is more﴾ of blessings which never occurred to their minds and never passed through their imagination.

Ibn Mardawayh has transmitted from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah descends upon the son of Adam in four stations: He is nearer to him than the jugular vein, He comes between a person and his heart, He holds the forelock of every creature, and He is with them wherever they are."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿the jugular vein﴾ that he said: the veins of the neck.
Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him that he said: it is the sinew of the heart.
Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, regarding His saying ﴿He does not utter a word except that with him is an watchful observer, ready﴾: he said: He records everything he says, good or evil, to the extent that he records his saying: "I ate, I drank, I went, I came, I saw." Then when Thursday comes, his saying and his deed are presented, and what was good or evil of it is confirmed, and the rest is discarded. That is His saying: ﴿Allah erases what He wills and establishes﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39].

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through the chain of ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: only good and evil are recorded; it does not record "O boy, saddle the horse" or "O boy, give me water."

It is established in the Two Sahihs and others from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah has forgiven this community what its souls speak of, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from ʿAmr ibn Dharr who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah is at the tongue of every speaker, so let a servant fear Allah and let him watch what he says."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), the like of it.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th, and Ibn ʿAsakir transmitted from ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan that he recited ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness﴾ and said: the driver drives it to the command of Allah, and the witness testifies against it for what it did.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th transmitted from Abu Hurayrah regarding the verse that he said: the driver is the angel, and the witness is the deed.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: the driver is from among the angels, and the witness is a witness against him from his own self.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him regarding ﴿You were certainly heedless of this﴾ that he said: it refers to the disbeliever.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him ﴿So We have removed from you your covering﴾, he said: it is life after death.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, and ﴿His companion will say﴾, he said: his devil.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim, regarding His saying ﴿Do not dispute before Me﴾, said: they offered excuses without a valid excuse, so Allah refuted their argument and rejected their saying.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾, he said: I do not punish one who has not committed a crime.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿On the Day when We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾, he said: "Is there any place in me that can be added to me?"

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others transmitted from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hell will continue to have people cast into it, and it will say, 'Is there any more?' until the Lord of Might places His foot in it, and then some of it will draw in upon others, and it will say: 'Enough, enough, by Your might and Your generosity.' And Paradise will continue to have surplus, until Allah creates for it another creation, and He will settle them in the surplus of Paradise."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim also transmitted a similar hadith from Abu Hurayrah, and there are other hadiths on this topic.

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿for every returning penitent, observant﴾, he said: he guarded his sins until he turned back from them.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa'l-Nushur transmitted from Anas, regarding His saying ﴿And with Us is more﴾, he said: (p-1402) the Lord, Blessed and Exalted, manifests Himself to them every Friday.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Ru'yah and al-Daylami transmitted from ʿAli regarding the verse that he said: the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, manifests Himself to them. There are other hadiths on this topic.

[p. 1399]

His words: ﴿Indeed, We created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him﴾. This is a new statement that contains a mention of part of God's power. By "man" is meant the species, though it has been said that it refers to Adam. Al-waswasah (whispering) is originally a faint sound, and here it means what stirs in his secret thoughts, his heart, and his inner self. That is, We know what he conceals and harbours within his soul. An example of using waswasah for a faint sound is the verse of al-A'sha:

*You hear the jingling of the anklets as she turns away*

So it was used for what is hidden in the speech of the soul. ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾. This is the vein of the shoulder, which extends from the side of his throat to his shoulder. These are two veins, one on the right and one on the left.

Al-Hasan said: al-Warid is al-Watain (the aorta), which is a vessel attached to the heart.

This is an illustration of nearness by the nearness of that vessel to the human being. That is: We are nearer to him than the vein of his jugular. The construction is explanatory (idafah bayaniyyah, a construction in which the second noun specifies the first): that is, a vein which is the warid.

It has been said that al-habl (the vein) is the same as al-warid, so it is like masjid al-jami' (the congregational mosque).

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned that, along with His knowledge of it, He has appointed for him two angels who record and preserve his deeds against him, as a means of establishing the proof. So He said: ﴿When the two receivers receive﴾. The adverbial phrase *idh* (when) is governed by the sense of the verb contained in *aqrab* (nearer). It is also permissible for it to be governed by an implied verb, *udhkur* (mention). The meaning is: He is nearer to him than the vein of his jugular when the two receivers receive. They are the two angels appointed over him, for whatever he utters and whatever he does. That is, they take that down and record it.

*Al-talaqqi* means taking. That is: We are most knowing of his circumstances, not needing the guardians appointed over him.

We made that as a means of establishing the proof and of emphasising the matter.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Mujahid said: "The two receivers are two angels who receive your deeds, one of them on your right, recording your good deeds, and the other on your left, recording your evil deeds."

Mujahid also said: God has appointed for the human being two angels by night and two by day, who guard his deeds and record their effects. ﴿On the right and on the left, one seated﴾. He said *qa'id* (seated) and did not say *qa'idan* (two seated), though they are two, because the meaning is: on the right, a seated one, and on the left, a seated one. So the first was omitted because the second indicates it. This is what Sibawayh said, like the words of the poet:

*We are with what we have, and you are with what you have, content, though the opinion differs.*

And the words of al-Farazdaq:

*And he came, and he was, and I was, not one to excuse.*

That is: "and he was not one to excuse, and I was not one to excuse." Al-Akhfash and al-Farra' said: the word *qa'id* is suitable for the singular, the dual and the plural, and needs no implied element in the first case.

Al-Jawhari and others among the imams of language and grammar said: *fa'il* and *fa'ul* are forms in which the singular, the dual and the plural are alike. *Al-qa'id* means one who sits, like *al-jalis* in the sense of *al-mujalis* (companion).

﴿He does not utter a word but there is with him a watchful observer, ready﴾. That is: he does not speak any speech, uttering it and casting it from his mouth, but with the one who utters it there is a watcher. That is: an angel who watches his words and records them. *Al-raqib* (watcher) is the one who preserves and follows the affairs of the human being, who records what he says of good and evil.

So the recorder of good is the angel of the right, and the recorder of evil is the angel of the left.

*Al-'atid* is the present and prepared one. Al-Jawhari said: *al-'atid* is the present and prepared one. It is said: *'attadahu ta'tidan* and *a'taddahu i'tidadan*, that is, he prepared it. From this is the verse ﴿and she prepared for them a couch﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. What is meant here is that he is made ready for writing and prepared for it.

﴿And the agony of death has come in truth﴾. When He, glorified is He, made clear that all his deeds are preserved and recorded, He mentioned after it what befalls them of death. By *sakratu al-mawt* (the agony of death) is meant its severity and its overwhelming, which covers the human being and overcomes his reason. The meaning of *bi'l-haqq* (in truth) is that at death the truth becomes clear to him, and the truthfulness of what the messengers brought of reports about resurrection, promise and threat becomes manifest to him. It has been said: the truth is death. It has also been said that there is inversion in the speech: that is, "the agony of the truth has come with death." Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Ibn Mas'ud also read it this way.

*Al-sakrah* is the truth, and it is attributed to itself because the two wordings differ. It has been said that the *ba'* (with) is for accompaniment, as in His words ﴿grows with oil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20]. That is: accompanied by the truth, that is, by the reality of the situation. The indication in His words *dhalika* (that) refers to death. *Al-hayd* is inclination. That is: that death, from which you used to incline and flee. It is said: *hada 'an al-shay'* yahidu huyudan, hayduda and hidah, meaning he inclined from it and turned aside. From this is the words of Tarafah:

*O Abu Munthir, you desired fidelity, so you feared it, and you swerved as the camel swerves from the slippery ground.*

Al-Hasan said: *tahid* means *tahrub* (flees).

﴿And the Trumpet is blown﴾. He expressed it in the past tense because its occurrence is certain. This is the final blast for resurrection. ﴿That is the Day of the Threat﴾. That is: that time, in which the blowing of the Trumpet occurs, is the Day of the Threat which God threatened the disbelievers with.

Muqatil said: by the threat is meant the punishment in the Hereafter. He singled out the threat, although the day is both the Day of Promise and of Threat, to magnify its terror.

﴿And every soul comes, with it a driver and a witness﴾. That is: every soul of the souls comes with someone who drives it and someone who bears witness for it or against it.

They differed about the driver and the witness. Al-Dahhak said: the driver is from among the angels, and the witness is from among themselves: that is, their hands and feet.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: a driver who drives it, and a witness who bears witness against it for its deeds.

Ibn Muslim said: the driver is its companion from among the devils; he is called a driver because he follows it, even if he does not urge it on.

Mujahid said: the driver and the witness are two angels.

It has been said: the driver is the angel, and the witness is the deed. It has been said: the driver is the recorder of evil deeds, and the witness is the recorder of good deeds. The clause occupies the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿You were heedless of this﴾. That is, it will be said to him: "You were heedless of this." The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from *nafs* (soul), or it is a new clause, as if it were said: "what is said to him."

Al-Dahhak said: by "this" is meant the polytheists, because they were heedless of the consequences of their affairs.

Ibn Zayd said: the address is to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): that is, "You were, O Muhammad, heedless of the message."

Most of the commentators said: what is meant is all creation, the righteous and the wicked among them, and Ibn Jarir chose this view.

The majority read *kunta* with a *fatha* on the *ta'* and *ghita'aka* and *basaruka* with a *fatha* on the *kaf*, in accordance with the masculine wording of *kull* (every).

Al-Jahdari and Talhah ibn Musarrif read with a *kasrah* throughout, on the basis that what is meant is the soul (nafs, feminine).

﴿So We have removed from you your covering﴾, which was in the world. That is: We removed the veil that was between you and the affairs of the Hereafter, and removed your heedlessness of that. ﴿So your sight today is sharp﴾. That is: penetrating, by which you see what was hidden from you of the world.

Al-Suddi said: by the covering is meant that he was in his mother's womb and then was born. It has been said that he was in the grave and then was raised. The first is preferable.

As for *al-basar* (sight), it has been said it is the sight of the heart, and it has been said it is the sight of the eye.

Mujahid said: your sight is directed at the tongue of your scale when your good and evil deeds are weighed. Al-Dahhak also said this.

﴿And his companion says: "This is what I have ready"﴾. That is: the angel appointed over him says: "This is what I have from the book of your deeds, ready, present, which I have prepared." So said al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

Mujahid said: the angel says to the Lord, glorified is He: "This is the one You appointed me over from the children of Adam; I have brought him and brought the register of his deeds."

It is related from him that he said: his companion is from the devils, and he says this: that is, "This is what I have prepared for you by my seduction and misguidance."

Ibn Zayd said: what is meant here is his companion from mankind. *'Atid* is in the nominative case as an attribute of *ma* (what), if it is a qualified noun; if it is a relative, it is a predicate after a predicate, or the predicate of an implied subject.

﴿Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever﴾. This is an address from God, mighty and majestic, to the driver and the witness.

Al-Zajjaj said: this is a command to the two angels appointed over him, who are the driver and the witness: "every disbeliever in blessings, stubborn, turning away from faith."

﴿Hindering the good﴾, not spending any good; ﴿transgressing, a doubter﴾, one who does not acknowledge the unity of God; ﴿doubting﴾, uncertain about the truth, from their saying *arāba al-rajul*, when a man became one who has doubt.

It has been said: this is an address to the two angels of the guards of the Fire.

It has been said: this is an address to one person, with the dual of the agent being treated as the dual of the verb and its repetition.

Al-Khalil and al-Akhfash said: this is the correct usage of the Arabs, that a single person is addressed with the dual form. They say *irhalaha*, *izjuraha*, *khudhahu*, *atliqahu*, to a single person.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say to a single person *quma 'anna* (stand away from us).

The origin of this is that the least of a man's helpers with his camels, sheep and companions on a journey are two. So the speech of a man to one person proceeded in accordance with that. From it is the saying of the Arabs to one person in poetry, as Imru' al-Qays said:

*O my two friends, pass by me over Umm Jundab, so we may soothe the bindings of the tormented heart.*

And his words:

*Stop, let us weep for the memory of a beloved and a dwelling, at the edge of al-Liwa, between al-Dukhul and Hawmal.*

And the words of another:

*If you two rebuke me, O son of Affan, I will be rebuked; and if you two call me, I will protect an honour that is defended.*

Al-Mazini said: His words *alqiya* (cast, dual) indicate *alqi alqi* (cast, cast). Al-Mubarrad said: it is a dual for emphasis, so *alqiya* stands in place of *alqi alqi*.

Mujahid and Ikrimah said: *al-'anid* is the one who opposes the truth. It has been said: the one who turns away from the truth. It is said: *'anada ya'nidu* with *kasrah*, *'unudan*, when he opposed the truth.

﴿Who set up with God another god﴾. It may be a substitute for *kull* (every), or an accusative in dispraise, or a substitute for *kaffar* (disbeliever), or nominative as a subject, or the predicate. ﴿So cast him into the severe punishment﴾. This is an emphasis of the first command, or a substitute for it.

﴿His companion says: "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress; but he was in far-off error"﴾. This clause is a new statement explaining what the companion says. By the companion here is meant the devil who was assigned to this disbeliever. He denied that he had caused him to transgress. Then he said: ﴿but he was in far-off error﴾: that is, far from the truth; so I called him and he responded to me; had he been one of Your sincere servants, I would not have been able to overcome him. It has been said that his companion is the angel who used to record his evil deeds, and that the disbeliever says: "Lord, he hastened me," and He answers him with this. Thus said Muqatil and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The first is preferable, and the majority held it.

﴿He says: "Do not dispute before Me"﴾. This clause is a new statement answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did God say?" So it is said: ﴿He says: "Do not dispute before Me"﴾, meaning the disbelievers and their companions. He, glorified is He, forbade them to dispute at the place of reckoning. The clause ﴿and I had already sent to you the threat﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, while the situation is that I had already sent to you the threat by sending the messengers and revealing the books. The *ba'* in *bil-wa'id* (with the threat) is extra for emphasis, or it is based on taking *qaddama* (sent forward) to mean *taqaddama* (went forward).

﴿The word is not changed before Me﴾. That is: there is no breaking of My promise; rather it is certain to occur, and I have decreed punishment upon you, so there is no altering of it. It has been said: this word is His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever brings an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 50, verse 16–35 (part 2 of 2):

It was said: it is His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ [Hud: 119]. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of the verse is that "the word is not altered in My presence by addition to it or subtraction from it, because of My knowledge of the unseen." This is the view of al-Kalbi, and al-Wahidi preferred it, because He said "with Me" (ladayya) and did not say "and My word is not changed." The first view is more preferable. It was also said: the object of ﴿I have already sent forth to you﴾ is ﴿the word is not altered﴾, i.e., "I have already sent forth to you this saying accompanied by the threat." This is very far-fetched. ﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾, i.e., I do not punish them unjustly, without a crime they committed or a sin they perpetrated. Since negating ẓallām (one who wrongs greatly) does not necessitate negating mere injustice (ẓulm), it was said that it here carries the meaning of ẓālim (wrongdoer), like tammār in the sense of tāmir (date-seller). It was also said: the intensive form is to emphasize this meaning by presenting the mentioned punishment without a sin in the context of exaggeration in injustice. It was also said: the intensive form is to observe the plurality of the servants, from the saying of people: "So-and-so is unjust to his servant" and "ẓallām to his servants." It was said other than this as well. The discussion of this has already passed in Surat Āl ʿImrān and Surat al-Ḥajj.
