Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it means in seclusion, where no one sees him.
Al-Hasan said: when he draws the curtain and closes the door.
(The phrase "in the unseen") is related to an elided element that is in the state position, or an adjective of the verbal noun of khashiya (fear). ﴿And comes with a heart turning (in repentance)﴾, i.e., returning to Allah, sincere in obedience to Him. It was said: al-munīb is the one who turns to obedience. It was said: it is the sound one.
"Enter it" is with the implied verb: i.e., it is said to them, "Enter it." The plural is according to the meaning of "man" (min). I.e., enter Paradise in peace, meaning in safety from punishment. It was said: in peace from Allah and His angels. It was said: in safety from the cessation of blessings. This is related to an elided element in the state position: i.e., accompanied by peace. The reference in His saying ﴿That﴾ is to the time of that day, as Abu al-Baqa' said, and its predicate is ﴿the Day of Eternity﴾. He called it the Day of Eternity because it has no end; rather it is everlasting forever.

﴿For them is whatever they wish therein﴾, i.e., in Paradise is whatever their souls desire and their eyes delight in, of the varieties of blessings and kinds of good. ﴿And with Us is more﴾ of blessings which never occurred to their minds and never passed through their imagination.

Ibn Mardawayh has transmitted from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah descends upon the son of Adam in four stations: He is nearer to him than the jugular vein, He comes between a person and his heart, He holds the forelock of every creature, and He is with them wherever they are."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿the jugular vein﴾ that he said: the veins of the neck.
Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him that he said: it is the sinew of the heart.
Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, regarding His saying ﴿He does not utter a word except that with him is an watchful observer, ready﴾: he said: He records everything he says, good or evil, to the extent that he records his saying: "I ate, I drank, I went, I came, I saw." Then when Thursday comes, his saying and his deed are presented, and what was good or evil of it is confirmed, and the rest is discarded. That is His saying: ﴿Allah erases what He wills and establishes﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39].

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through the chain of ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: only good and evil are recorded; it does not record "O boy, saddle the horse" or "O boy, give me water."

It is established in the Two Sahihs and others from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah has forgiven this community what its souls speak of, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from ʿAmr ibn Dharr who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah is at the tongue of every speaker, so let a servant fear Allah and let him watch what he says."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), the like of it.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th, and Ibn ʿAsakir transmitted from ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan that he recited ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness﴾ and said: the driver drives it to the command of Allah, and the witness testifies against it for what it did.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th transmitted from Abu Hurayrah regarding the verse that he said: the driver is the angel, and the witness is the deed.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: the driver is from among the angels, and the witness is a witness against him from his own self.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him regarding ﴿You were certainly heedless of this﴾ that he said: it refers to the disbeliever.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him ﴿So We have removed from you your covering﴾, he said: it is life after death.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, and ﴿His companion will say﴾, he said: his devil.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim, regarding His saying ﴿Do not dispute before Me﴾, said: they offered excuses without a valid excuse, so Allah refuted their argument and rejected their saying.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾, he said: I do not punish one who has not committed a crime.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿On the Day when We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾, he said: "Is there any place in me that can be added to me?"

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others transmitted from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hell will continue to have people cast into it, and it will say, 'Is there any more?' until the Lord of Might places His foot in it, and then some of it will draw in upon others, and it will say: 'Enough, enough, by Your might and Your generosity.' And Paradise will continue to have surplus, until Allah creates for it another creation, and He will settle them in the surplus of Paradise."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim also transmitted a similar hadith from Abu Hurayrah, and there are other hadiths on this topic.

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿for every returning penitent, observant﴾, he said: he guarded his sins until he turned back from them.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa'l-Nushur transmitted from Anas, regarding His saying ﴿And with Us is more﴾, he said: (p-1402) the Lord, Blessed and Exalted, manifests Himself to them every Friday.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Ru'yah and al-Daylami transmitted from ʿAli regarding the verse that he said: the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, manifests Himself to them. There are other hadiths on this topic.

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah 50, verses 36–45:

God warned the people of Makkah with what befell the generations before them, that is, before Quraysh and those who agreed with them, from a *qarn* (a generation or nation), namely a people: ﴿They were mightier than them in strength﴾, that is, in power, like ʿĀd, Thamūd and others. ﴿So they ransacked the lands﴾, that is, they traveled and roamed through them and went about their regions. Its root is from *naqb*, which is a path.

Mujāhid said: "They struck (the land) and went about."

Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: "They went around."

Al-Mu'arrij said: "They went far away."

The first meaning is the better one, and from it comes the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"I have ransacked the horizons until I was content with the spoil of returning."*

Similar to it is the saying of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza:

*"They ransacked the lands out of fear of death, and roamed every place in the earth."*

Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, and Abū ʿAmr, in one narration, read *naqabū* with a fatḥah on the qāf and no doubling. *Al-naqb* is a hole or breach, and a path through a mountain. Likewise *al-manqab* and *al-manqabah*. Thus said Ibn al-Sikkīt. The plural of *al-naqb* is *nuqūb*.

Al-Sulamī and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar read *naqqibū* with a kasrah on the qāf and doubling, as an imperative of threat: that is, "Go about in them and travel through their sides."

The rest read it with a fatḥah on the qāf and doubling, as a past tense. ﴿Is there any escape?﴾ That is: Is there any way of flight for them to flee to, or any way of deliverance by which they might be freed from the punishment?

Al-Zajjāj said: "They saw no escape from death." *Al-maḥīṣ* is the verbal noun of *ḥāṣa ʿanhu, yaḥīṣu, ḥaydan, ḥuyūṣan, maḥīṣan, maḥāṣan, ḥayaṣānan*, meaning he deviated and swerved. The clause is independent, explaining that they have no escape. In this there is a warning to the people of Makkah that they are like those generations before them, who find no refuge from death and punishment.

﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder﴾, that is, in what has been mentioned of their story there is a reminder and an admonition, ﴿for whoever has a heart﴾, that is, intellect.

Al-Farrāʾ said: "This is permissible in Arabic. You say: 'You have no heart, and your heart is not with you,' meaning: you have no intellect, and your intellect is not with you." It has also been said that the intended meaning is the heart itself, because when it is sound it perceives realities and reflects as it should.

It has also been said: for whoever has life and a discerning self. This is expressed by "heart" because it is the home of the self and the source of its life. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Did it deceive you about me that your love would kill me, and that whatever you command the self, it will do?"*

﴿Or gives ear﴾, that is, listens to what is said to him. It is said: "Give your ear to me," meaning: listen to me. The meaning is that he gives ear to what is recited to him of the revelation that tells what happened to those nations.

The majority read *alqā* in the active voice.

Al-Sulamī, Ṭalḥah, and al-Suddī read it in the passive voice, with *al-samʿ* in the nominative.

﴿And he is a witness﴾, that is, present in understanding or present in heart, because whoever does not understand is in the status of an absent person, even if he is present bodily; he is not present with his understanding.

Al-Zajjāj said: "That is, his heart is present in what he hears."

Sufyān said: "That is, he is not present while his heart is absent."

Mujāhid and Qatādah said: this verse is about the People of the Book. Al-Ḥasan also said this.

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb and Abū Ṣāliḥ said: it is specifically about the People of the Qur'an.

﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾. The interpretation of this verse has already been given in Surat al-Aʿrāf and elsewhere. ﴿And no weariness touched Us﴾. *Al-lughūb* is fatigue and exhaustion. It is said: *laghiba yalghubu*, with a ḍammah, *lughūban*.

Al-Wāḥidī said: A group of commentators said: The Jews said: "God created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, the first of which was Sunday and the last of which was Friday, and He rested on Saturday." So God refuted them by His saying: ﴿And no weariness touched Us. So be patient over what they say﴾, as a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ), and He commanded him to be patient over what the polytheists say, that is: ease your mind, do not grieve over their words, and meet what comes to you from them with patience. ﴿And glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾, that is: exalt God above what is not fitting for His lofty majesty, joined with His praise, at the time of Fajr and the time of ʿAṣr. It has been said: the intended meaning is the Fajr prayer and the ʿAṣr prayer. It has been said: the five prayers. It has been said: pray two rakʿahs before sunrise and two rakʿahs before sunset. The first view is the better one.

﴿And of the night, glorify Him﴾. *Min* here is partitive, meaning: glorify Him during part of the night. It has been said: this is the night prayer. It has been said: the two rakʿahs of Fajr. It has been said: the ʿIshāʾ prayer. The first view is the better one. ﴿And the adbār of the prostrations﴾, that is, glorify Him after the prayers.

The majority read *adbāra* with a fatḥah on the hamzah, as the plural of *dubur*.

Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, and Ḥamzah read it with a kasrah, as a verbal noun from *adbara al-shayʾu, idbāran*, when it turns away.

A group of the Companions and the Successors said: *Idbār al-sujūd* is the two rakʿahs after Maghrib, and *Idbār al-nujūm* is the two rakʿahs before Fajr.

The Seven Readers (*al-qurrāʾ al-sabʿah*) agreed on *wa-idbāra al-nujūm* with a kasrah on the hamzah, as will come later.

﴿And listen on the day the caller calls from a near place﴾, that is, listen to what is revealed to you about the conditions of the Resurrection, on the day the caller calls. He is Isrāfīl, or Jibrīl. It has been said: listen to the call, or the sound, or the Blast, which is the blast of the Resurrection, namely the second blowing into the Trumpet by Isrāfīl. It has been said: Isrāfīl blows, and Jibrīl calls out to the people of the gathering, saying: "Come to the reckoning." On this view the calling is in the place of gathering.

Muqātil said: It is Isrāfīl who calls for the gathering, saying: "O people, come to the reckoning." ﴿From a near place﴾, in such a way that the call reaches every single individual among the people of the gathering.

Qatādah said: We used to hear that he calls from the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis.

Al-Kalbī said: It is the nearest point of the earth to the heaven, by twelve miles.

Kaʿb said: by eighteen miles.

﴿On the day they hear the Blast in truth﴾. This is a substitute for "the day the caller calls," meaning the Blast of resurrection. *Bi-al-ḥaqq* is connected to *al-ṣayḥah*. ﴿That is the day of coming out﴾, that is, the day of coming out from the graves.

Al-Kalbī said: The meaning of *bi-al-ḥaqq* is "with the resurrection."

Muqātil said: It means that it is definitely going to happen.

﴿Indeed, We give life and cause death﴾, that is, We give life in the Hereafter and cause death in this world, and no associate shares with Us in that. The clause is independent, establishing the matter of resurrection. ﴿And to Us is the final return﴾, so that We reward every doer for his deed.

﴿On the day the earth splits open from them﴾. The majority read it with the *tāʾ* assimilated into the *shīn*. The Kufans read it with the *shīn* lightened, by deleting one of the two *tāʾs* for ease. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read *tatashaqqaq* with both *tāʾs* retained, as in the original form. It was also read in the passive voice. *Sirāʿan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the pronoun in *ʿanhum*. The governing element of the state is *tashaqqaq*. It has been said that the governing element of the state is the same as that governing *yawma*, meaning: hastening toward the caller who called them. ﴿That is a gathering﴾, that is, a resurrection and a assembling. ﴿For Us it is easy﴾, effortless.

Then God, glorified is He, consoled His Prophet (ﷺ) and said: ﴿We know best what they say﴾, meaning of your denial of what you have brought, and of their denial of the resurrection and of monotheism. ﴿And you are not over them a tyrant﴾, that is, not one empowered to compel them and force them to faith. The verse is abrogated (*mansūkhah*, subject to *naskh*) by the verse of the sword. ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾, that is, whoever fears My warning to My disobedient servants with punishment. As for those other than them, do not concern yourself with them. Then God, glorified is He, after that commanded him to fight.

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And no weariness touched Us﴾ that he said: "From fatigue."

Al-Ṭabarānī in *al-Awsaṭ* and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿And glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun﴾: the Ṣubḥ prayer, ﴿and before the setting﴾: the ʿAṣr prayer.

al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "I spent the night with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he prayed two light rakʿahs before the Fajr prayer. Then he went out to the prayer and said: 'O Ibn ʿAbbās, two rakʿahs before the Fajr prayer are *idbār al-nujūm*, and two rakʿahs after Maghrib are *idbār al-sujūd*.'"

Musaddad in his *Musnad*, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who said: "I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about *idbār al-nujūm* and *idbār al-sujūd*, and he said: '*Idbār al-sujūd* is the two rakʿahs after Maghrib, and *idbār al-nujūm* is the two rakʿahs before the dawn (*al-ghadāh*).'"

al-Bukhārī and others narrated from Mujāhid, who said: Ibn ʿAbbās said: "He was commanded to glorify Him after all the prayers."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from him regarding ﴿And listen on the day the caller calls﴾ that he said: "It is the Blast."

al-Wāsiṭī also narrated from him ﴿from a near place﴾ that he said: "From the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis."

Al-Mu'arrij said: "They went far away."

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah 50, verses 36–45:

God warned the people of Makkah with what befell the generations before them, that is, before Quraysh and those who agreed with them, from a *qarn* (a generation or nation), namely a people: ﴿They were mightier than them in strength﴾, that is, in power, like ʿĀd, Thamūd and others. ﴿So they ransacked the lands﴾, that is, they traveled and roamed through them and went about their regions. Its root is from *naqb*, which is a path.

Mujāhid said: "They struck (the land) and went about."

Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: "They went around."

Al-Mu'arrij said: "They went far away."

The first meaning is the better one, and from it comes the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"I have ransacked the horizons until I was content with the spoil of returning."*

Similar to it is the saying of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza:

*"They ransacked the lands out of fear of death, and roamed every place in the earth."*

Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, and Abū ʿAmr, in one narration, read *naqabū* with a fatḥah on the qāf and no doubling. *Al-naqb* is a hole or breach, and a path through a mountain. Likewise *al-manqab* and *al-manqabah*. Thus said Ibn al-Sikkīt. The plural of *al-naqb* is *nuqūb*.

Al-Sulamī and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar read *naqqibū* with a kasrah on the qāf and doubling, as an imperative of threat: that is, "Go about in them and travel through their sides."

The rest read it with a fatḥah on the qāf and doubling, as a past tense. ﴿Is there any escape?﴾ That is: Is there any way of flight for them to flee to, or any way of deliverance by which they might be freed from the punishment?

Al-Zajjāj said: "They saw no escape from death." *Al-maḥīṣ* is the verbal noun of *ḥāṣa ʿanhu, yaḥīṣu, ḥaydan, ḥuyūṣan, maḥīṣan, maḥāṣan, ḥayaṣānan*, meaning he deviated and swerved. The clause is independent, explaining that they have no escape. In this there is a warning to the people of Makkah that they are like those generations before them, who find no refuge from death and punishment.

﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder﴾, that is, in what has been mentioned of their story there is a reminder and an admonition, ﴿for whoever has a heart﴾, that is, intellect.

Al-Farrāʾ said: "This is permissible in Arabic. You say: 'You have no heart, and your heart is not with you,' meaning: you have no intellect, and your intellect is not with you." It has also been said that the intended meaning is the heart itself, because when it is sound it perceives realities and reflects as it should.

It has also been said: for whoever has life and a discerning self. This is expressed by "heart" because it is the home of the self and the source of its life. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Did it deceive you about me that your love would kill me, and that whatever you command the self, it will do?"*

﴿Or gives ear﴾, that is, listens to what is said to him. It is said: "Give your ear to me," meaning: listen to me. The meaning is that he gives ear to what is recited to him of the revelation that tells what happened to those nations.

The majority read *alqā* in the active voice.

Al-Sulamī, Ṭalḥah, and al-Suddī read it in the passive voice, with *al-samʿ* in the nominative.

﴿And he is a witness﴾, that is, present in understanding or present in heart, because whoever does not understand is in the status of an absent person, even if he is present bodily; he is not present with his understanding.

Sufyān said: "That is, he is not present while his heart is absent."

Mujāhid and Qatādah said: this verse is about the People of the Book. Al-Ḥasan also said this.

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb and Abū Ṣāliḥ said: it is specifically about the People of the Qur'an.

It was also read in the passive voice. *Sirāʿan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the pronoun in *ʿanhum*. The governing element of the state is *tashaqqaq*. It has been said that the governing element of the state is the same as that governing *yawma*, meaning: hastening toward the caller who called them. ﴿That is a gathering﴾, that is, a resurrection and a assembling. ﴿For Us it is easy﴾, effortless.

Then God, glorified is He, consoled His Prophet (ﷺ) and said: ﴿We know best what they say﴾, meaning of your denial of what you have brought, and of their denial of the resurrection and of monotheism. ﴿And you are not over them a tyrant﴾, that is, not one empowered to compel them and force them to faith. The verse is abrogated (*mansūkhah*, subject to *naskh*) by the verse of the sword. ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾, that is, whoever fears My warning to My disobedient servants with punishment. As for those other than them, do not concern yourself with them. Then God, glorified is He, after that commanded him to fight.

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And no weariness touched Us﴾ that he said: "From fatigue."

Al-Ṭabarānī in *al-Awsaṭ* and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿And glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun﴾: the Ṣubḥ prayer, ﴿and before the setting﴾: the ʿAṣr prayer.

al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "I spent the night with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he prayed two light rakʿahs before the Fajr prayer. Then he went out to the prayer and said: 'O Ibn ʿAbbās, two rakʿahs before the Fajr prayer are *idbār al-nujūm*, and two rakʿahs after Maghrib are *idbār al-sujūd*.'"

Musaddad in his *Musnad*, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who said: "I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about *idbār al-nujūm* and *idbār al-sujūd*, and he said: '*Idbār al-sujūd* is the two rakʿahs after Maghrib, and *idbār al-nujūm* is the two rakʿahs before the dawn (*al-ghadāh*).'"

Muḥammad ibn Naṣr in *al-Ṣalāh*, and Ibn al-Mundhir, narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb: "*Idbār al-sujūd* is two rakʿahs after Maghrib, and *idbār al-nujūm* is two rakʿahs before Fajr."

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn Naṣr, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Asmāʾ wa-al-Ṣifāt* narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib something similar.

al-Bukhārī and others narrated from Mujāhid, who said: Ibn ʿAbbās said: "He was commanded to glorify Him after all the prayers."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from him regarding ﴿And listen on the day the caller calls﴾ that he said: "It is the Blast."

al-Wāsiṭī also narrated from him ﴿from a near place﴾ that he said: "From the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him as well ﴿That is the day of coming out﴾ that he said: "The day they come out to the resurrection from the graves."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from him as well, who said: "They said: 'O Messenger of God, if only you would warn us.' So there was revealed: ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾."

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah 50, verses 36–45:

God warned the people of Makkah with what befell the generations before them, that is, before Quraysh and those who agreed with them, from a *qarn* (a generation or nation), namely a people: ﴿They were mightier than them in strength﴾, that is, in power, like ʿĀd, Thamūd and others. ﴿So they ransacked the lands﴾, that is, they traveled and roamed through them and went about their regions. Its root is from *naqb*, which is a path.

Mujāhid said: "They struck (the land) and went about."

Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: "They went around."

Al-Mu'arrij said: "They went far away."

The first meaning is the better one, and from it comes the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"I have ransacked the horizons until I was content with the spoil of returning."*

Similar to it is the saying of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza:

*"They ransacked the lands out of fear of death, and roamed every place in the earth."*

Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, and Abū ʿAmr, in one narration, read *naqabū* with a fatḥah on the qāf and no doubling. *Al-naqb* is a hole or breach, and a path through a mountain. Likewise *al-manqab* and *al-manqabah*. Thus said Ibn al-Sikkīt. The plural of *al-naqb* is *nuqūb*.

Al-Sulamī and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar read *naqqibū* with a kasrah on the qāf and doubling, as an imperative of threat: that is, "Go about in them and travel through their sides."

The rest read it with a fatḥah on the qāf and doubling, as a past tense. ﴿Is there any escape?﴾ That is: Is there any way of flight for them to flee to, or any way of deliverance by which they might be freed from the punishment?

Al-Zajjāj said: "They saw no escape from death." *Al-maḥīṣ* is the verbal noun of *ḥāṣa ʿanhu, yaḥīṣu, ḥaydan, ḥuyūṣan, maḥīṣan, maḥāṣan, ḥayaṣānan*, meaning he deviated and swerved. The clause is independent, explaining that they have no escape. In this there is a warning to the people of Makkah that they are like those generations before them, who find no refuge from death and punishment.

﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder﴾, that is, in what has been mentioned of their story there is a reminder and an admonition, ﴿for whoever has a heart﴾, that is, intellect.

Al-Farrāʾ said: "This is permissible in Arabic. You say: 'You have no heart, and your heart is not with you,' meaning: you have no intellect, and your intellect is not with you." It has also been said that the intended meaning is the heart itself, because when it is sound it perceives realities and reflects as it should.

It has also been said: for whoever has life and a discerning self. This is expressed by "heart" because it is the home of the self and the source of its life. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Did it deceive you about me that your love would kill me, and that whatever you command the self, it will do?"*

﴿Or gives ear﴾, that is, listens to what is said to him. It is said: "Give your ear to me," meaning: listen to me. The meaning is that he gives ear to what is recited to him of the revelation that tells what happened to those nations.

The majority read *alqā* in the active voice.

Al-Sulamī, Ṭalḥah, and al-Suddī read it in the passive voice, with *al-samʿ* in the nominative.

﴿And he is a witness﴾, that is, present in understanding or present in heart, because whoever does not understand is in the status of an absent person, even if he is present bodily; he is not present with his understanding.

Al-Zajjāj said: "That is, his heart is present in what he hears."

Sufyān said: "That is, he is not present while his heart is absent."

Mujāhid and Qatādah said: this verse is about the People of the Book. Al-Ḥasan also said this.

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb and Abū Ṣāliḥ said: it is specifically about the People of the Qur'an.

﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾. The interpretation of this verse has already been given in Surat al-Aʿrāf and elsewhere. ﴿And no weariness touched Us﴾. *Al-lughūb* is fatigue and exhaustion. It is said: *laghiba yalghubu*, with a ḍammah, *lughūban*.

Al-Wāḥidī said: A group of commentators said: The Jews said: "God created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, the first of which was Sunday and the last of which was Friday, and He rested on Saturday." So God refuted them by His saying: ﴿And no weariness touched Us. So be patient over what they say﴾, as a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ), and He commanded him to be patient over what the polytheists say, that is: ease your mind, do not grieve over their words, and meet what comes to you from them with patience. ﴿And glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾, that is: exalt God above what is not fitting for His lofty majesty, joined with His praise, at the time of Fajr and the time of ʿAṣr. It has been said: the intended meaning is the Fajr prayer and the ʿAṣr prayer. It has been said: the five prayers. It has been said: pray two rakʿahs before sunrise and two rakʿahs before sunset. The first view is the better one.

﴿And of the night, glorify Him﴾. *Min* here is partitive, meaning: glorify Him during part of the night. It has been said: this is the night prayer. It has been said: the two rakʿahs of Fajr. It has been said: the ʿIshāʾ prayer. The first view is the better one. ﴿And the adbār of the prostrations﴾, that is, glorify Him after the prayers.

The majority read *adbāra* with a fatḥah on the hamzah, as the plural of *dubur*.

Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, and Ḥamzah read it with a kasrah, as a verbal noun from *adbara al-shayʾu, idbāran*, when it turns away.

A group of the Companions and the Successors said: *Idbār al-sujūd* is the two rakʿahs after Maghrib, and *Idbār al-nujūm* is the two rakʿahs before Fajr.

The Seven Readers (*al-qurrāʾ al-sabʿah*) agreed on *wa-idbāra al-nujūm* with a kasrah on the hamzah, as will come later.

﴿And listen on the day the caller calls from a near place﴾, that is, listen to what is revealed to you about the conditions of the Resurrection, on the day the caller calls. He is Isrāfīl, or Jibrīl. It has been said: listen to the call, or the sound, or the Blast, which is the blast of the Resurrection, namely the second blowing into the Trumpet by Isrāfīl. It has been said: Isrāfīl blows, and Jibrīl calls out to the people of the gathering, saying: "Come to the reckoning." On this view the calling is in the place of gathering.

Muqātil said: It is Isrāfīl who calls for the gathering, saying: "O people, come to the reckoning." ﴿From a near place﴾, in such a way that the call reaches every single individual among the people of the gathering.

Qatādah said: We used to hear that he calls from the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis.

Al-Kalbī said: It is the nearest point of the earth to the heaven, by twelve miles.

Kaʿb said: by eighteen miles.

﴿On the day they hear the Blast in truth﴾. This is a substitute for "the day the caller calls," meaning the Blast of resurrection. *Bi-al-ḥaqq* is connected to *al-ṣayḥah*. ﴿That is the day of coming out﴾, that is, the day of coming out from the graves.

Al-Kalbī said: The meaning of *bi-al-ḥaqq* is "with the resurrection."

Muqātil said: It means that it is definitely going to happen.

﴿Indeed, We give life and cause death﴾, that is, We give life in the Hereafter and cause death in this world, and no associate shares with Us in that. The clause is independent, establishing the matter of resurrection. ﴿And to Us is the final return﴾, so that We reward every doer for his deed.
